description: Paint Your Truth: 6-Week Community Solidarity Series Join us in person for a fun and inspiring 6-week journey of creativity and connection! "Paint Your Truth" is all about coming together to express your unique story through art while building community solidarity. Whether you're a beginner or a pro, this series is a chill space to share, learn, and grow with others. Don't miss out on this chance to paint, laugh, and connect! This session focuses on reconnecting with your inner voice through process painting. Participants are invited to explore color, gesture, and emotion without judgment—giving themselves permission to express freely. We open with a welcoming circle, move through embodied warmups, and journey into two hours of supported painting time. This session sets the tone for the entire series: community, courage, vulnerability, and creative truth-telling. Jan 17, 2026 Week 2: Time: Rhythm & Creative Rituals Guest facilitator Missy Arellano, also known as The Clock Lady, joins Vie for a unique, time-centered creative exploration. Missy works with concepts of rhythm, duration, and personal cycles. Together, Vie and Missy guide participants through reflective prompts, meditative timed exercises, and creative rituals linked to personal and collective rhythms. Participants explore how time shapes their healing and how painting can become a grounding ritual that honors both slowness and momentum. Jan 24 2026 Week 3: Deepening Your Inner Narrative This solo-led session returns to the heart of Paint Your Truth: connecting to your story. Participants move deeper into their creative process with expanded prompts that explore memory, identity, and emotional layering. title: Belmont World Film's 23rd Family Festival: Day 4
description: Parents with children ages 3–12 won’t want to miss Belmont World Film’s 23rd Family Festival. Guided by this year’s theme Lights, Camera, Magic!, the festival showcases a diverse selection of films from around the world—many making their North American or U.S. premieres—offering young audiences an immersive and culturally rich cinematic experience. It’s a wonderful way to “travel the world” during MLK Weekend and beyond without the cost or hassle of a trip. The festival takes place at the West Newton Cinema from January 17–18, the Brattle Theatre on Monday, January 19, the Belmont Media Center on Saturday, January 24, and the Regent Theatre on Sunday, January 25. This year’s lineup includes mostly North American premieres, with more than half of the films adapted from or inspired by classic and contemporary children’s books—a longstanding festival hallmark. For young readers and those who struggle with reading, a professional voice-over will read subtitles aloud for films in languages other than English, creating an experience much like story time. Your children can also engage in hands-on workshops--including Learn to the Draw the Minions and Hotel Transylvania Characters and Introduction to Storyboarding for Animated Films--with this year’s Artists-in-Residence, story artist and director Dave Feiss and story artist and writer Paul McEvoy, both of whom have most recently worked on The SpongeBob Movie: Search for SquarePants, as well as the Minions and Hotel Transylvania franchises and many others. Purchase tickets in advance only at https://www.belmontworldfilm.org/family-festival or in person on day of show at the box office (cash only).
cost: Shorts programs: $8. Feature length films: $12. Workshops: $22. Films Only Pass: $40. VIP Full Access Pass: $100. Save $8 on 4-packs.

title: Harvard College Opera presents Mozart's Le Nozze di Figaro (The Marriage of Figaro)
description: Mozart’s comic opera, set in 18th-century Spain, follows a tumultuous day in the lives of Figaro and Susanna, servants in the household of Count Almaviva. As they prepare for their wedding, complications arise when the Count—tiring of his marriage to the Countess—schemes to seduce Susanna. Figaro, Susanna, and the Countess join forces to outwit him, while a host of subplots involving disguises, mistaken identities, and romantic entanglements add to the chaos. Join us for an unforgettable evening featuring some of the most famous operatic tunes! Performed in Italian with English supertitles.

title: MIT's Musical Theater Guild Presents: The Great Comet of 1812
description: From the celebrated and award-winning composer Dave Malloy comes Natasha, Pierre & The Great Comet of 1812, an electropop opera based on a scandalous slice of Leo Tolstoy’s War and Peace. Young and impulsive, Natasha Rostova arrives in Moscow to await the return of her fiancé from the front lines. When she falls under the spell of the roguish Anatole, it is up to Pierre, a family friend in the middle of an existential crisis, to pick up the pieces of her shattered reputation. Following a critically exalted premiere at Ars Nova in New York City, a subsequent off-Broadway transfer and an acclaimed run on Broadway, this award-winning musical expands the possibilities for the genre with its daring score and bold storytelling.

title: Community Education Event: ShotSpotter & Public Safety
description: On Wednesday, February 11, The Black Response (TBR), as part of the Stop ShotSpotter Camberville Coalition, will host a dinner and community education event at CIC in Kendall Square (245 Main Street, Cambridge) to examine the impacts of ShotSpotter, a network of highly sensitive microphones marketed as gunshot detection technology. While promoted as a public safety tool, ShotSpotter functions as a form of audio surveillance that is disproportionately deployed in Black and Brown neighborhoods (The Port and Riverside neighborhoods in Cambridge), raising serious concerns about privacy, accuracy, and the expansion of police surveillance. Locally, ShotSpotter microphones are funded through a grant from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the parent agency of ICE, heightening concerns for vulnerable community members who are undocumented, on Temporary Protected Status (TPS), or living under other tenuous immigration statuses at a time of increased ICE raids and federal policing violence. This raises urgent questions about federal overreach and the ability of the federal government to bypass local governance in a city that has committed to being a sanctuary city; through the welcoming city ordinances. At the event, Boston University Professor Spencer Piston will deliver a critical presentation on ShotSpotter, dispelling the company’s claims and explaining its local impacts. Cambridge and Somerville residents will also have the opportunity to share their perspectives through an anonymous survey. Free childcare will be provided. This event is co-sponsored by the SURJ Boston Prison Abolition Working Group, SURJ Boston, the Massachusetts Pirate Party, and Defund Somerville PD. Time: Doors open at 5:30 pm; Potluck dinner is at 6:00 pm to 8:00 pm. Bring a dish to share if you can. Free childcare provided. Registration: https://forms.gle/5QBESN6LoSLd9G6A8

title: Unleash Your Imagination: Exploring Creativity in the Age of AI
description: This hands-on workshop is for anyone (youth, parents, grandparents) who’s curious about what generative AI can do, what it can’t, and what about creativity is uniquely human. You don't need to be an artist or a technical expert - just an open mind, curiosity and a willingness to try something new. Through a combination of presentations and guided activities we'll learn about Generative AI, explore emerging trends, examine the growing tension between AI art and creative expression, what responsible use looks like and the ethical complexities that are frequently overlooked. You’ll start with your own imagination, see how AI interprets it, and then try to bring it to life. Join us at the Foundry Festival for an experimental and experiential evening filled with inquiry, creativity and imagination!

title: Anthony Dunne and Fiona Raby, "Unreal by Design"
description: According to an increasing number of theoretical physicists, spacetime might not be as fundamental as we think, and new theories could emerge that describe an even more fundamental reality, especially at the quantum scale. We find it fascinating that a concept we consider so essential to our understanding of reality might be nearing the end of its usefulness—a reminder that even our seemingly most stable intellectual structures are provisional and subject to revision. It feels like we are living in a moment when reality is beginning to exceed the human imagination, both politically, scientifically, and historically. By wrestling with the unthinkable and the impossible, we believe design can enable a more meaningful engagement with the strange reality unfolding around us, a world where doubt, uncertainty, and the unknowable are the new norms.

title: Boston Screening of The [M] Factor Film 2: Before the Pause (Perimenopause)
description: The Whiny GYNie and Women’s Health Advocates present The M Factor Film 2: Before the Pause (Perimenopause)—a Boston screening at MassArt’s Tower Auditorium on February 26, 2026, followed by a live panel and Q&A advancing women’s health equity. Join The Whiny GYNie and Women’s Health Advocates for The M Factor Film 2: Before the Pause (Perimenopause)—an educational evening designed to deepen understanding of perimenopause and the wide range of symptoms, experiences, and care pathways that too often go unrecognized. The film aims to demystify this life stage with clear, relatable storytelling that helps attendees better identify what’s happening in their bodies, find language to describe symptoms, and feel more prepared to navigate conversations about midlife health. Following the screening, we’ll host a live panel discussion and audience Q&A featuring a Menopause Society Certified OB/GYN and menopause advocates who will expand on the film’s themes, share practical guidance, and answer questions in real time. Whether you’re in the thick of perimenopause, supporting someone who is, or simply want a stronger foundation of knowledge, this event offers an approachable, empowering way to learn, connect, and leave with actionable takeaways. title: ShotSpotter: Dinner and Community Education
description: On Wednesday, March 4th, the Stop ShotSpotter Coalition Camberville will host a community education workshop on ShotSpotter. The event will feature presentations by Gabriel Rojas, University of Chicago doctoral candidate, and Valerie Werder, a doctoral candidate at Harvard University. Gabriel Rojas has conducted extensive research on ShotSpotter in Chicago. His presentation will examine the history of SoundThinking (formerly ShotSpotter), the logic and strategies for ShotSpotter’s implementation, and the legal and affective harms associated with the ShotSpotter system. Valerie Werder’s research critically examines police body camera footage. She explores the financialization of police body cameras, their implementation and governing protocols, and notably, the contractual terms surrounding data and access of police body cameras and footage. Her presentation will also reflect on the City of Boston’s 2013 contract with the corporation (then known as) ShotSpotter as well as a speculative analysis of how the ShotSpotter data might be used if the devices, the data, and financialization follows the trajectory of police body cameras. Please join us for a thought provoking set of presentations.

title: Zak Kyes, "Identity Crisis"
description: Design is not simply in crisis; it’s in an identity crisis—a profession uncertain of its purpose, value, and future. In this talk, Zak Kyes, founder and creative director of Zak Group, traces how design has historically metabolized moments of rupture: from the printing press to platform capitalism, from wartime propaganda to today’s prompt-driven production. Drawing on two decades of work across cultural institutions, fashion, and contemporary art, he shows how the sands have shifted: the mid-tier collapse, the acceleration of AI, and a profession increasingly compressed into speed, style—and little else. Drawing from recent projects with Nike, Dover Street Market, and others, Kyes introduces a set of practical frameworks he calls Crisis Overrides: tools for navigating uncertainty, protecting authorship, and reclaiming strategic agency at a moment when design’s relevance is no longer guaranteed. Part memoir, part manifesto, part diagnosis, “Identity Crisis” reframes instability as a generative condition, reminds us that the most vital designs have always emerged because of chaos, not in spite of it.
street_address: Gund Hall, 48 Quincy St, Cambridge, MA, 02138

title: Kenzie Bok, "The Past, Present, and Future of Public Housing"
description: In the 25th Annual John T. Dunlop Lecture , presented by the Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies , Kenzie Bok , CEO of the Boston Housing Authority and former Boston City Councilor, will bring together her experiences as a pioneering public housing administrator and intellectual historian to explore the past, present, and future of public housing in the United States. She will discuss how justice, fairness, and the role of government have shaped public housing, and how these ideas must evolve to meet today’s interconnected challenges of affordability, climate change, and inequality. Following the lecture, Chris Herbert , Managing Director of the Joint Center for Housing Studies, will moderate a conversation with Bok and Bernardo Zacka , an associate professor of political science at MIT, whose interests include the moral dilemmas that public service workers encounter when enacting public policy and how the architecture of welfare offices can shape interactions with citizens.
street_address: Gund Hall, 48 Quincy St, Cambridge, MA, 02138

description: BOSTON, MA – The Boston Wine Expo, New England's premier wine event, returns to Boston on March 7-8, 2026, bringing together over 100 wineries from around the globe for two days of wine discovery and education. With strong advance ticket sales and an impressive roster of international exhibitors, the 2026 expo promises to be the region's most diverse wine experience to date. Wine enthusiasts and industry professionals will have the opportunity to taste wines from some of the world's most celebrated regions, including Wines of Sicily, Wines of South Africa, Wines of Australia, the Côtes du Rhône region of France, and the prestigious Saint-Émilion appellation of Bordeaux. The expo will also feature a rare appearance by Golan Heights Winery from Israel, offering attendees a unique chance to explore emerging wine regions. "This year's Boston Wine Expo showcases the incredible diversity of the global wine industry," said Raffaele Scalzi, Director of the Boston Wine Expo. "We're thrilled to welcome both established wine regions and exciting new players to Boston, giving our guests the chance to discover wines they won't find anywhere else in New England."

title: Marina Otero Verzier, "Feral Clouds"
description: Feral Clouds draws on research supported by the Wheelwright Prize to examine the architectures and politics of data processing and storage in a context shaped by technological competition and climate collapse. Bringing together activism, policy work, design prototypes, and educational initiatives, this lecture proposes a reorientation of digital culture away from Cartesian paradigms and market-driven notions of efficiency. Ferality operates here as a lens through which to understand both the excesses of an industry obsessed with winning the AI race at the expense of the planet and the unruly consequences of that obsession. From the residual heat expelled by servers to the destruction embedded in AI supply chains, digital infrastructures generate effects that evade design, control, and prediction. At the same time, “ferality” refers to forms of contestation against this violence, as well as the unintended relationships and material transformations that fracture techno-solutionist imaginaries and give rise to alternative energy cultures. Drawing on sovereign and Indigenous clouds, feminist servers, permaculture imaginaries, and low-tech computation, Otero Verzier outlines speculative yet actionable directions for systems of data storage that embrace limits, decay, and transformation. Join us the next day, on March 10, for a conversation between Marina Otero Verzier and Kate Crawford that dives deeper into the questions Marina raises in her lecture.
street_address: Gund Hall, 48 Quincy St, Cambridge, MA, 02138

title: Conversation with Marina Otero Verzier & Kate Crawford
description: In 2022, Marina Otero Verzier was named the winner of the Wheelwright Prize, a grant to support investigative approaches to contemporary architecture with an emphasis on globally-minded research. In her winning proposal, Future Storage: Architectures to Host the Metaverse, Otero examined new architectural paradigms for storing data and how reimagining digital infrastructures could meet the unprecedented demands facing the world today. The resulting field research, data collection, and prototype development point towards alternative models for global data centers, including examples of ecological, circular, and egalitarian data storage models. As with past Wheelwright winners, the prize funded two years of Otero’s research and travel. After presenting her project in a lecture on March 9, “Feral Clouds,” Otero will dive deeper into the questions and implications of her research the next day in a conversation with AI scholar and artist Kate Crawford.

title: Boston Festival Orchestra: Brahms in Boston
description: The Boston Festival Orchestra launches its Season 6 Chamber Series with an evening of music rooted in New England voices and landscapes, presented for the first time at the First Church in Cambridge. Together, these works explore memory, place, and personal expression across generations. Join BFO Artistic Director Alyssa Wang, BFO musicians, and guest artists for an immersive chamber music experience that blends performance with thoughtful discussion, inviting audiences to engage with the music’s historical, cultural, and emotional context. title: Chatpong Chuenrudeemol, "Bangkok Bastards"
description: “Bangkok Bastards” are works of everyday architecture created by everyday people to solve everyday problems. From temporary construction worker houses to illegal shantytowns to underground sex-motels, these vernacular spaces are scattered throughout Thailand’s capital. Bastards are constructed with inexpensive, locally sourced, and often scavenged materials in simple yet ingenious ways. Due to their illegitimate origins and “cheap” appearance, Bastards are dismissed as low-brow, unrefined, dirty scars in the city, unworthy of serious research. However, Chuenrudeemol sees them as honest, clever, and improvisational responses to the city’s challenges, and perhaps the most authentic and relevant examples of vernacular architecture in Thailand’s urban landscape. Chatpong Chuenrudeemol’s “Bastards research” is the foundation on which his office, CHAT Architects, develops its projects. Through a process called “Bastardizing the Bastard,” CHAT creates new, locally rooted hybrids by crossbreeding, transforming, and combining existing Bastards with newly invented programs and other urban, social, and ecological dilemmas. This lecture will also explore the firm’s recent efforts to expand its research into the Thai countryside, in search of “Rural Crossbreeds.”

title: Michael Wang Lecture
description: Michael Wang uses systems that operate at both regional and planetary scales as media for art, addressing climate, ecology, extraction, and capital. His works include Extinct in the Wild, a project onspecies that exist only under human care; 10000 li, 100 billion kilowatt-hours, which harnessed Shanghai’s hydropower-fueled electric grid to create a frozen facsimile of the glaciers at the origin of the Yangtze river; First Forest, a Carboniferous forest installed in a disused coal-gas plant; and, Carbon Copies, an exhibition linking the production of artworks to the release of greenhouse gases—envisioning all artists as “air artists.” Wang was awarded the Joan Mitchell Foundation Painters & Sculptors Grant, and his work was the subject of solo exhibitions at Prada Rong Zhai, Shanghai (2022), LMCC’s Arts Center at Governors Island, New York (curated by the Swiss Institute, 2019) and the Fondazione Prada, Milan (2017). His work was also included in Planetary Peasants at Kunstmuseum Moritzburg Halle (2025), Elevation 1049 in Gstaad, Switzerland (2023), the 13th Shanghai Biennale (2021), Manifesta 12 Palermo (2018), and the XX Bienal de Arquitectura y Urbanismo in Valparaíso (2017). This event is part of ArtsThursdays, a university-wide initiative supported by Harvard University Committee on the Arts (HUCA).

title: Blindfolded Bicycle Ride for the Boston Fringe Festival
description: UNCLE YAK TO DEFY COMMON SENSE WITH BLINDFOLDED BIKE RIDE IN DAVIS SQUARE Somerville, MA — In a daring blend of illusion, optimism, and extremely casual risk assessment, local magician and theatrical phenomenon, Uncle Yak, will ride a bicycle blindfolded through Davis Square, starting and ending in front of The Rockwell theater. The audacious feat will announce his upcoming appearance in the Boston Fringe Festival and promote his show, Uncle Yak and his Magic Comeback. But this is not merely a stunt. It is an experiment in collective belief, performance art, eco-friendly transportation, and cardiovascular exercise. Uncle Yak claims the ride will only be possible through the focused positive will of the crowd, who will be asked to concentrate, cheer, and project supportive thoughts in his direction to “guide the bicycle using vibes alone.” “Technically, I will be steering with the handlebars,” says Uncle Yak, “but spiritually, the audience will be steering with their hearts.” “If enough people believe in me at once,” he explains, “the bike will simply know where to go. It’s like a self-driving car, but the tech is the magic that flickers deep inside every one of us. Like, you know, hopefully.” “Some performers hang posters,” Uncle Yak adds. “I ride blindly into destiny. But I will probably hang some posters too.” The event is designed to celebrate the joyful chaos of the Boston Fringe Festival and draw attention to Uncle Yak’s one-man show, Uncle Yak and his Magic Comeback, a high-energy mix of comedy, illusion, and theatrical nonsense about rust, relevance, and making a comeback that no one asked for, but everyone will enjoy. Uncle Yak and his Magic Comeback will be performed at the Boston Fringe Festival at The Rockwell on Thursday, May 14 at 9:15pm, Saturday, May 16 at 7:05pm, and Sunday, May 17 at 8:10pm

title: Boston Climate Week Event: Companies Leading the Way on Climate Solutions
description: ​​Sustainserv is a Boston-based sustainability consulting firm with offices in Boston, Frankfurt, and Zurich. Boston-based companies have long been meaningfully engaged in sustainability efforts, and more recently, aggressive efforts to reduce their impacts on climate change. In the course of doing so, they have spear-headed innovative approaches to energy efficiency, circularity and creative approaches to financing sustainability efforts just to name a few. ​Join Sustainserv on May 7 at The Foundry in Cambridge for a session where some of the thought leaders of the Boston corporate sustainability scene discuss their efforts to combat climate change, talk about the challenges and opportunities, and to help chart the course forward in these dynamic times. ​A wine/beer reception will follow to cap off the session. ​SPEAKERS ​Cristina Mendoza, Sustainserv Director, will lead a panel with corporate Sustainability leaders including: ​ Julie Kae, Qlik Technologies ​Alyssa Caddle, Thermo Fisher ​Danielle Ricketts, Kindercare ​Clare Connolly, Eversource ​ ​This event is free entry with limited tickets available

title: Vijay Iyer and Wadada Leo Smith: Defiant Life
description: Composer-pianist Vijay Iyer and composer-trumpeter Wadada Leo Smith perform their duo creations, developed over 20 years of collaboration. Two of creative music’s most heralded luminaries, each feted with prizes and critical accolades from across the globe, composer-pianist Vijay Iyer and composer-trumpeter Wadada Leo Smith construct powerful, uncategorizable duets full of subtle emotion, mystery, and spiritual intensity. Their music reveals the improvisational magic of the duo, the expressive individuality of the participants, and the ways that they can – as Smith says – “merge as a single wave, or a single voice.” This event is part of ArtsThursdays, a university-wide initiative supported by Harvard University Committee on the Arts (HUCA). title: Make Me Famous Film Screening
description: Boston PREMIERE of critically acclaimed Art Documentary, Make Me Famous. Certified Fresh 100% on Rotten Tomatoes Make Me Famous is a vibrant, fast-paced portrait of New York City’s explosive 1980s Downtown art scene—where punk met paint, and the lines between art, music, and nightlife blurred. This was the world that launched Jean-Michel Basquiat, Keith Haring, Madonna, and Blondie—a cultural moment defined by its grit, glamour, and DIY ethos. Amid the chaos was painter Edward Brezinski, a figure both present and peripheral, whose story offers a unique window into the era’s creative frenzy. More than a portrait of an artist, Make Me Famous captures a time and place where the dream of making it felt just within reach—and heartbreakingly out of grasp. Filmmaker Q&As after the screening. 5/14 Moderated by Ezra Haber Glenn from MIT and the Boston Society of Film Critics

Once a beloved performer across the Northeast, Uncle Yak returns to the stage after years of PTA meetings, office coffee pods, and whatever else passes for adulthood. His new PG-13 show is a celebration of chance, persistence, and the joy of the unexpected. Is he too old? Have his magical powers dried up? Was he ever any good? Find out as Uncle Yak wrestles with rust, relevance, and ridiculousness as he attempts the impossible: a comeback no one asked for, but all will enjoy. title: Be a Phoenix: A Tribute to Gazan Poet Heba Al-Madhoun
description: Be a Phoenix: A Tribute to Gazan Poet Heba Al-Madhoun Sunday, June 7 @ 3:30 PM EDT The Foundry, 101 Rogers St, Cambridge, MA 02142 Speaker: Middle East Institute Senior Fellow and Yale Peace Fellow Jaser AbuMousa *Register here*: https://givebutter.com/heba-memorial About the Tribute: Poet and novelist Heba Al-Madhoun was an architect and educator, an avid collector of copperware, a passionate textiles artisan, and a loving wife and mother. On October 15, 2023, she was killed by an Israeli airstrike, alongside two of her four children, her sister and nephew. Join us in honoring Heba and her surviving family at a reading of her poems, newly translated into English by a Boston community initiative. title: U.S. Premiere of the Film Documentary 'Hope'
description: Join community members for the exclusive U.S. premiere of Hope, a powerful independent documentary exploring the resilience, daily lives, and profound human stories of refugees who have fled to Uganda to escape the civil war in South Sudan. Rather than viewing the circumstances through a lens of tragedy, the film highlights their aspirations and hopes for their futures, as well as an enduring desire to see justice in their homeland. The June 18 screening at the historic Capitol Theatre marks the very first time the film will be shown to audiences in the United States. Following the film, attendees are invited to stay for an interactive discussion and Q&A with our guest, Mr. Brian Adeba, a former refugee from Sudan and now serving as Advisor, Sudan & South Sudan at The Sentry. description: Please join us the Margaret Fuller Neighborhood House on July 11th for Port Community Pride Day, a free event for neighbors, friends, and family in and around Cambridge! Every summer since its inception in 2002, Port Community Pride Day has brought together residents, community organizations, civic leaders, and neighbors from across Cambridge for a free, full-day celebration hosted by the Margaret Fuller Neighborhood House in collaboration with community partners throughout The Port. Reflecting the spirit of the neighborhood it celebrates, the event includes a basketball tournament, community resource fair, live entertainment, free food, and community activities. description: Dance For The Diaspora (D4D Boston) is a citywide celebration of movement, music, cultural memory, wellness, and collective care featuring workshops, performances, community activations, conversations, DJs, and immersive artistic experiences across Boston and New England. Rooted in Black, Indigenous, diasporic, and LGBTQ+ cultural practices, D4D brings together artists, culture bearers, organizers, and community members to gather, move, learn, and imagine together. Supported by NEFA’s Public Art for Spatial Justice initiative, D4D explores how public art and collective gathering can help create more just, connected, and community-centered public spaces. Developed in partnership with Museum of African American History, Multicultural Arts Center, and The Haus of Glitter, the festival is part of an ongoing residency supporting the development of The Historical Fantasy of Boston. title: Poetry Reading: Tracy K. Smith
description: The Longfellow Summer Arts Festival brings music, poetry, and community to the East Lawn of the Longfellow House on Sunday afternoons through the summer. All events are free and open to the public. This reading is presented in partnership with the New England Poetry Club. Tracy K. Smith is a Pulitzer Prize-winning poet, memoirist, editor, translator and librettist. She served as the 22nd Poet Laureate of the United States from 2017-19, during which time she spearheaded American Conversations: Celebrating Poetry in Rural Communities with the Library of Congress, created the American Public Media podcast The Slowdown, and edited the anthology American Journal: Fifty Poems for Our Time. Smith is the author of five poetry collections: Such Color: New and Selected Poems, which won the 2022 New England Book Award; Wade in the Water, which was awarded the 2018 Anisfield-Wolf Book Award; Life on Mars, which won the 2012 Pulitzer Prize; Duende, winner of the 2006 James Laughlin Award of the Academy of American Poets; and The Body’s Question, which received the 2003 Cave Canem Prize. Her memoir, Ordinary Light, was a finalist for the 2015 National Book Award in nonfiction. She is the co-translator (with Changtai Bi) of My Name Will Grow Wide like a Tree: Selected Poems of Yi Lei, which was a finalist for the 2021 Griffin Poetry Prize; and co-editor (with John Freeman) of There’s a Revolution Outside, My Love: Letters from a Crisis. Her memoir-manifesto, To Free the Captives: A Plea for the American Soul, was a Time magazine and Washington Post Best Book of the Year, and a New York Times Book Review Editors' Choice. Fear Less: Poetry in Perilous Times is a nonfiction celebration of poetry as a source of courage and emotional fortitude amidst the many upheavals of the 21st Century. She is the Boylston Professor of Rhetoric and Oratory at Harvard University, and a Susan S. and Kenneth L. Wallach Professor at Harvard Radcliffe Institute.

title: Headquarters of a Revolution: Washington’s Arrival in Cambridge
description: Explore the people, ideas, and questions that shaped General George Washington’s first revolutionary headquarters 251 years ago this July. Choose your path through this free, all-ages event featuring historic house and outdoor walking tours; family activities; film screenings; living historians, a Story Walk, and more. Free and open to all! The house at 105 Brattle Street, now Longfellow House-Washington’s Headquarters National Historic Site, served as Washington’s first military headquarters of the American Revolution from July 1775-March 1776. Headquarters was a testing ground for many of the ideals, institutions, and questions that still define our country. This event will reveal Cambridge Headquarters as a complex hub of revolutionary activity, where generals, enslaved people, paid laborers, poets, Indigenous diplomats, politicians, self-emancipated families, and soldiers shaped history.

It’s also a participatory science event where we collect, record, photograph, and identify moths while learning more about their extraordinary lives. Explore the many hands-on activities offered by our partner organizations and get to know moths up close as we share the data and photos we collect with researchers. It’s also part of National Moth Week. This year, we also celebrate the power of moths to inspire the creative imagination of artists. If you’re interested in nature, insects, butterflies, moths, native plants, pollinators, or the amazing wildlife of Cambridge—or if you simply enjoy nighttime, nerding out, and learning something new—this event is for you. He is also an Assistant Professor at Berklee College of Music, where he teaches courses on performance and spoken word poetry, and an Instructor at Clark University in Worcester, where he teaches the introduction to poetry. He founded the LiteraryMusic Ensemble Neon JuJu: a literary and musical arts ensemble utilizing classic, contemporary and original literary text combined with Middle Eastern, Contemporary American and European classic music. Regie is widely published in anthologies, magazines and journals such as The Iowa Review, Harvard Divinity Magazine, Poetry Magazine, Spoken Word Revolution (Source Books), The Good Men Project and several others. description: The Longfellow Summer Arts Festival brings music, poetry, and community to the East Lawn of the Longfellow House on Sunday afternoons through the summer. Major Jackson is the author of six books of poetry, including Razzle Dazzle: New & Selected Poems (Blue Flower Arts, 2023), The Absurd Man (W.W. Norton & Company, 2020), Roll Deep (W.W. Norton & Company, 2015), Holding Company (W.W. Norton & Company, 2010), Hoops (W.W. Norton & Company, 2006), and Leaving Saturn (University of Georgia Press, 2002), which won the Cave Canem Poetry Prize for a first book of poems. Jackson’s edited volumes include Best American Poetry 2019 (Scribner), Renga for Obama (Harvard Review Monographs, 2017), and the Library of America’s Countee Cullen: Collected Poems (2013). He is also the author of A Beat Beyond: Selected Prose of Major Jackson, edited by Amor Kohli (University of Michigan Press, 2022). A recipient of fellowships from the Fine Arts Work Center in Provincetown, Guggenheim Foundation, National Endowment for the Arts, and Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study at Harvard University, Major Jackson was awarded a Pushcart Prize and a Whiting Award and received honors from the Pew Fellowship in the Arts and the Witter Bynner Foundation in conjunction with the Library of Congress. He has published poems and essays in American Poetry Review, The New Yorker, Orion magazine, the Paris Review, Ploughshares, Poetry magazine, Poetry London, and ZYZZYVA. Major Jackson lives in Nashville, Tennessee, where he is the Gertrude Conaway Vanderbilt Chair in the Humanities at Vanderbilt University. He hosts The Slowdown podcast, a partnership between the Poetry Foundation and American Public Media, and is poetry editor of the Harvard Review.

title: Golden Rose Award (Poetry): Marie Howe
description: The Longfellow Summer Arts Festival brings music, poetry, and community to the East Lawn of the Longfellow House on Sunday afternoons through the summer. All events are free and open to the public. This reading is presented in partnership with the New England Poetry Club. Marie Howe, recipient of the 2026 Golden Rose Award for Poetry, is the author of New and Selected Poems, (W.W. Norton 2024.) which includes poems from her four previous books. From 2012-2014, she served as the Poet Laureate of New York State. She is the poet in residence at The Cathedral Church of St. John the Divine, and a chancellor of the Academy of American Poets. Marie Howe's The Good Thief (1988), was chosen for the National Poetry Series by Margaret Atwood, who praised Howe’s “poems of obsession that transcend their own dark roots.” In that collection, Howe’s oracular yet self-doubting speakers often voice their concerns through Biblical and mythical allusions. Kunitz, on selecting the book for the Lavan Younger Poets Prize from the American Academy of Poets, observed, “Her long, deep-breathing lines address the mysteries of flesh and spirit, in terms accessible only to a woman who is very much of our time and yet still in touch with the sacred.” Howe has taught at Sarah Lawrence College, Columbia University, and NYU. She coedited (with Michael Klein) the essay anthology In the Company of My Solitude: American Writing from the AIDS Pandemic (1994). She has received fellowships from the Bunting Institute at Radcliffe College, the National Endowment for the Arts, the Guggenheim Foundation, the Academy of American Poets, and the Fine Arts Work Center in Provincetown. She was the Poet Laureate of New York State from 2012 to 2014. She is the poet in residence at The Cathedral Church of St. John the Divine and a chancellor of the Academy of American Poets. Howe lives in New York City.

title: Concert: Yujin Han
description: The Longfellow Summer Arts Festival brings music, poetry, and community to the East Lawn of the Longfellow House on Sunday afternoons through the summer. All events are free and open to the public. This concert is presented in partnership with the Berklee Summer in the City concert series. Yujin Han, a South Korea-born jazz pianist, composer, and arranger, studied at Dongduk Women’s University in Korea. She started her career as the leader of an alternative R&B band, the Blowers, in 2020. She developed a distinctive compositional voice with the support of the CJ Cultural Foundation, presenting her music to public audiences. After moving to the United States, she continued her studies at Berklee College of Music with the support of a Presidential Scholarship. At the Berklee Global Jazz Institute and the Berklee Institute of Jazz and Gender Justice, she deepened her exploration of creative harmonic approaches and rhythms, drawing inspiration from diverse global musical influences. She has performed at Panama Jazz Festival, Medford Jazz Festival, Boston Progressive Jazz Festival, and a variety of venues in Korea and Boston. She was featured as an emerging artist at the 2024 Vermont Solo Jazz Piano Festival.

description: Some evenings entertain. The Velvet Hour invites you into another world. Join Little Miss and the Boom at Crystal Ballroom for a two-hour modern vintage cabaret where live music, theatrical storytelling, glamour, and unexpected moments unfold throughout the evening. This is not a traditional concert. It’s an immersive experience designed to transport you from the moment the lights dim until the final encore. The night features Little Miss and the Boom’s signature blend of swing, blues, jazz, and modern vintage favorites, presented in a carefully crafted theatrical production that moves from intimate and sultry to playful, exhilarating, and unforgettable. Adding to the evening, acclaimed burlesque artist Pixie Payne joins the cast for an exclusive performance created especially for The Velvet Hour, seamlessly woven into the night’s story. Whether you’re dressed in vintage glamour or simply looking for an extraordinary night out, you’ll find yourself part of an experience where the audience isn’t just watching the show, they’re inside it. The Evening Includes: • A two-hour live cabaret experience with Little Miss and the Boom • Special guest performance by acclaimed burlesque artist Pixie Payne • Carefully crafted theatrical moments throughout the evening • VIP Velvet Tables available with premium seating, early entry, and a signed copy of Betwixt and Between concert poster • Vintage-inspired attire encouraged. Dress to be seen. One room. One evening. One unforgettable chapter. Welcome to The Velvet Hour.

description: 2026 LILA Dance Festival by LILA Productions The sixth annual Lila Dance Festival to take place at Rochester Commons featuring dance, live music, food, vendors and more. Rochester, NH – June 30, 2026 — Lila Dance Festival, New Hampshire’s largest dance festival will take place Saturday, August 29th from 12pm noon to 8pm at Rochester Commons Park with a Sunday, August 30th rain date. Entry is free and attendees are encouraged to bring their own chairs and blankets to enjoy the festival and events throughout the day. The program will feature a diverse range of dance styles, including ballet, contemporary, modern, jazz, tap, hip hop, cultural dance forms, and more, including a performance by returning guest artist Yuval Cohen. title: Concert: Pete Smith
description: The Longfellow Summer Arts Festival brings music, poetry, and community to the East Lawn of the Longfellow House on Sunday afternoons through the summer. All events are free and open to the public. Pete Smith is a New York City-based guitarist (and H.W. Longfellow descendant) who performs in a wide range of musical settings. As a founding member of Grupo los Santos (Santos4tet), a vanguard Afro-Cuban and Brazilian-style quartet, he has played New York’s Town Hall and concerts throughout the U.S., Cuba & Austria. He has performed at the Berlin Jazz Festival and Montreal Jazz Festival, as well as concerts in thirty countries throughout Europe, Eastern Europe, Africa and Asia. He has worked with Norah Jones, trumpeter Donald Byrd, Cuban trombone master Juan Pablo Torres, Andrew Hill, Kat Edmonson, Vince Giordano & the Nighthawks, the Moonlighters, Madeline Peyroux, Natalie Merchant and Huun-Huur-Tu, and is a member of Michael Feinstein’s Carnegie Hall Big Band. In 2023 he traveled to Congo-Kinshasa (DRC) as a member of the band Opius Bliss—as cultural ambassadors for the US Embassy—to perform for and teach, play and dialogue with local musicians in Kinshasa and Kisangani. 2023 also saw the release of Santos4tet's 4th album "Santos 4". In 2024, Santos4tet was the recipient of a JazzRoad Touring Grant from SouthArts, funded by the Doris Duke Foundation and the Mellon Foundation, which supported their 5-city tour of the Sountheast. Pete will be recording a new album with bassist Sean Smith (The Smith Duo) in 2025.

title: Capital One Café Financial Firsts Mixer
description: On September 5, The Capital One Café at Harvard Square is helping to give students what they want and grow their financial confidence. Whether they bank with Capital One or not, everyone is welcome to join the free and interactive Financial Firsts Mixer: Level up your money game before the fall semester kicks into high gear. Managing your own finances for potentially the first time can be a big change, but it doesn't have to be intimidating. Stop into the Café for a fun activity designed to provide you with potential strategies for navigating this time of financial change and grow your financial confidence. You’ll complete our "build-a-kit" circuit across four interactive zones in the Café while tackling an experiential monthly budget simulation, setting attainable financial goals, and assembling your own First-Year Essentials Kit along the way. Grab a handcrafted beverage, sit down with your peers and our friendly Ambassadors, and pick up some tips and tricks for managing your financial future. title: Intro to Editing
description: Four session workshop introducing Adobe Premiere: Tuesdays 5:30 to 7:30 - September 8, 15, 22, and 29. No matter what type of video you want to make, editing is key. Being able to edit is an incredible skill to have, and in this class, you will learn the art and science of editing through Adobe Premiere Pro, the editing software considered the gold standard by independent filmmakers everywhere. By the end of the course, you will be able to cut and sequence footage to tell the story you want, and alter its aesthetic to create the look and sound you desire for your project. You’ll also learn to manage and organize files to ensure a smooth workflow every time. No experience is necessary and beginners are welcomed, as is anyone with experience in other editing softwares who would like to transfer their skills to Adobe Premiere Pro! Week 1: Learning the layout of the interface, how to create and open a project, import footage and access it on the timeline, organization of material Week 2: Cutting and extending clips, dissolves and transitions, adding audio, workflow Week 3: Color correction, audio mixing, captions, graphics, exporting Week 4: Bringing it all together/Final Project

title: New Exhibition + Artist Talk, Steve Rosenthal at Paul Dietrich Galler
description: The Paul Dietrich Gallery at CambridgeSeven opened its fall exhibition, A Symphony in Brick: Photography by Steve Rosenthal, on September 14. The show celebrates the architectural legacy of Haverhill’s Washington Street Shoe District through striking images of its Queen Anne and Italianate brickwork. This marks Rosenthal’s third solo presentation at the gallery and a creative homecoming, as he began his career at CambridgeSeven in 1965 before becoming a nationally recognized architectural photographer. The exhibition is presented in collaboration with Historic New England. EXHIBITION HIGHLIGHTS: Visual Storytelling of Virtuosity in Brick – See Rosenthal’s latest work, which captures the rich stories of the collaboration between skilled 19th century architects and craftsmen via photographs that detail masterful patterns and textures in brickwork. Artist Talk — Hear directly from Rosenthal about his latest project at the Opening Reception on September 17. He will be joined by Vin Cipolla, President and CEO of Historic New England, who will speak about Historic New England’s Haverhill initiative.

title: Voices for Ukraine
description: One evening. Three movements. Where human rights, health, scholarship, and culture meet in support of Ukraine. Voices for Ukraine: Symposium & Concert—a special evening convening internationally recognized leaders in human rights, global affairs, academia, mental health, humanitarian response, and the arts, alongside musicians and storytellers whose work carries Ukraine's voice into the world. The evening will also mark the public launch of First Aid of the Soul's Arts & Health Initiative in Ukraine, expanding our work at the intersection of mental health, the arts, and community wellbeing through partnerships with universities, healthcare institutions, and cultural organizations across the country.

title: Outdoor Movie Night: Toy Story 4
description: Join us in Canal Park at CambridgeSide for the final movie of our Outdoor Summer Movie Series. Join us for a fun-filled evening starting at 7pm. Kick things off with a creative Make Your Own Forky craft. After the activities, settle in for a screening of Toy Story 4, and finish the night with glow sticks as the sun goes down. It’s a playful summer night the whole family will enjoy. Grab a bite at CanalSide Food + Drink and join us on the lawn. Pre-show entertainment begins at 7pm. Movies begin promptly at 8pm . Plus, enjoy delicious popcorn sponsored by East Cambridge Business Association. Got school supplies? Bring them along! We will be collecting school supplies to benefit the East End House. Suggested donations include new and unused backpacks, pencils & pencil sharpeners, notebooks, binders and more. For all movie nights, attendees are encouraged to bring blankets or lawn chairs. Events are free and open to the public. All event elements are first come, first served basis. While supplies last. Please note: all minors must be accompanied by an adult.

title: Fitness Fest
description: Join us for Fitness Fest on September 19 from 11AM-2PM in Canal Park at CambridgeSide. Enjoy free, beginner-friendly fitness classes, live music from DJ J-Wall, lawn games, giveaways, and more, all in a beautiful waterfront setting. Local fitness partners will lead a variety of short, beginner-friendly fitness classes, stretching sessions, and movement activities designed for all ages and fitness levels.

title: Reducing the Risk of Nuclear War: The Long View
description: Some of the most consequential decisions our civilization makes — decisions that will shape the lives of countless future generations — concern nuclear weapons and the risk of nuclear war. Harvard's Matthew Bunn will join Long Now Boston to take the long view on one of humanity's defining challenges.

title: Somerville Garden Club Plant Sale
description: Discover the perfect plant to enliven your garden or windowsill at this popular yearly sale. Perennials for sun and shade, herbs, shrubs, groundcovers, plus a wide variety of house plants will be featured. Choose from hundreds of plants donated by Somerville Garden Club members and friends – there’s something for everyone! Horticultural books, decorative containers, and garden tools will also be for sale. Experienced gardeners will be available to answer questions and assist with plant selections. Proceeds benefit the all-volunteer, non-profit Somerville Garden Club.

title: Gymnastics Is for EveryBODY: Free Adult Open House at MIT (18+)
description: The name says it all: gymnastics is for Every—BODY. Come learn how EveryBODY Gymnastics makes gymnastics accessible and fun. Our programming is based on the teaching of beginner adult gymnastics pioneer Abbie Green, who still leads the program. Maybe you’ve always wanted to try gymnastics. Maybe you did it years ago and have missed it ever since. Maybe you’re an experienced gymnast looking for a community that sees the joy, curiosity, and possibility in movement—not a “right” body type or a required level of experience. Join us for a free adult Open House at MIT’s duPont Gymnasium. Adults 18+ are welcome, from first-time beginners to experienced gymnasts. No prior experience is required—just come ready to move, explore, and have fun. Doors open at 2:00 PM; Open House activities run from 2:15–4:15 PM. Event Details, Registration, and More About EBG: https://everybodygymnastics.wixsite.com/home/ebg-open-house

description: Free coding classes every Monday and Wednesday, 5:30 - 8 pm. Bring a laptop and work at your own pace on web development (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React) or Python, with volunteer developers helping at the table. Complete beginners, experienced developers and anyone looking for a friendly place to cowork are welcome. Pizza at 6:30. Ground floor common area - look for the table with the event poster. If the weather is nice, we meet just outside the library main entrance. No registration needed. Kids are welcome - parents stay with them. title: Chicken Wire Empire at Club Passim
description: CWE continuously captivates audiences with thoughtful, energetic performances. Their high-level musicality turns up a fresh conversation with each show, like a brainstorm of creative musical substance. Americana Highways writes “These musicians must enjoy what they do because their joy translates through their instruments. The energy, fingering techniques are all proponents that deliver substance with a modicum of joy. There aren’t any low points, missteps, loss of heat in any of these melodies.” The band has been recognized worldwide for their performances and recorded works, with Americana UK calling their latest album “a variety which transcends genre and rewards careful listening.” Capturing the ever-evolving sights and sounds of the road through the lens of their Midwestern roots, the band’s catalog of songs is ever-growing and CWE continues to be acknowledged for their pensive attention to detail in writing and crafting deeply engaging songs.

title: All We Are
description: Spanning generations and continents, the composers on this program ask what it means to endure, to hold multiple identities, and to cherish what is most fragile and fleeting. All We Are honors moments, both ordinary and remarkable, whose significance is often only understood in hindsight. Featuring works by Kian Ravaei, Reena Esmail, and David Biedenbender, and a world premiere by Oliver Caplan. With performances by Julia Scott Carey, Celine Ferro, Nicholas Johnson, and Kelley Hollis.

title: Harvard + Netflix Event: East of Eden
description: The Harvard Foundation and Office for the Arts invite you to an upcoming campus event featuring a Harvard alum, Hoon Lee ’94. On Tuesday, October 6, we’ll celebrate Netflix's adaptation of East of Eden (premiering October 1). We are excited to welcome Hoon Lee ('94), who stars as Lee in the series. (He also stars as Barney Choi in “Your Friends and Neighbors” on Apple TV.) Joining him will be co-showrunner, writer, and executive producer Zoe Kazan, alongside English professor Ju Yon Kim, for an engaging discussion on the series adaptation and Asian and Asian-American representation on screen.

title: Midday Music with Joseph Ntaimo
description: Enjoy music by Joseph Ntaimo, an MIT graduate student studying mechanical engineering with a focus in musical robotics. Alongside an upbeat DJ set, Ntaimo will play a ferro-instrument (a hyperinstrument that makes ferrofluid respond to music by altering the magnetic field) and other experimental musical devices he’s developing.

title: Music Bingo at CanalSide Every Wednesday
description: Get ready to tap your toes and test your musical knowledge with Music Bingo every Wednesday from 6pm to 8pm located in CanalSide Food + Drink. The first round starts promptly at 6:30pm. In this exciting twist on traditional bingo, letters and numbers are replaced with song titles and artists. Players mark off songs on their bingo cards as songs are played, competing to win based on their music knowledge and the unpredictability of the game. Featuring diverse rounds of music that showcase decades, genres, and themes, Musical Bingo brings sing-alongs galore and an unbeatable blend of fun and chance—mark your card, get five in a row, and yell BINGO to claim victory! Come early to grab a bite to eat and a drink from the dynamic C-Side Bar. One bingo card per person per round. Participants can only win once per event date.

title: How "The Raven" Became America's Most Famous Poem
description: Join us for this special book launch event with author Paul Lewis, on the 177th anniversary of the day Poe died in 1849. Copies of Quothing "The Raven": The First Responses to America's Most Famous Poem will be available for purchase and signing. What factors influenced the attention devoted to Poe's "Raven" from the very day when it was first published in 1845? Why was it widely reprinted, praised, criticized, and mocked during the following weeks and months? How has it sustained interest from that first publication through to the present? And how did Poe's "Little Longfellow War" and Bostonian parodies of "The Raven" figure in the rollicking rollout of America's most famous poem? Blurbs: "Paul Lewis's QUOTHING 'THE RAVEN' is a wonderful romp through the sea of parodies that proliferated in the wake of the publication of Edgar Allan Poe's 'The Raven' in 1845. Here we meet not the saintly, stately Raven of Poe's poem, but 'The Owl,' 'The Turkey,' 'The Gazelle,' and even 'The Bed Bug.' Gathering these parodies together for the first time, Lewis expertly guides readers through the chaotic world of Antebellum magazines and newspapers that Poe himself navigated. Lewis has written an absolutely delightful book full of both humor and wisdom about America's most famous poem." --Sandra Tomc, professor of English Language and Literature, University of British Columbia, Vancouver, and author of INDUSTRY AND THE CREATIVE MIND "QUOTHING 'THE RAVEN' is a significant contribution to Poe scholarship and a genuine pleasure to read. Poe said that he wrote his most famous poem 'for the express purpose of running,' and Paul Lewis shows us how it 'ran' through 1840s pop culture and reshaped Poe’s career and reputation. The parodies themselves are fascinating, and the context Lewis provides for them is invaluable. This book is essential to understanding how 'The Raven' became America's favorite poem." --Scott Peeples, author of THE MAN OF THE CROWD and THE AFTERLIFE OF EDGAR ALLAN P

For more information call McCarthy's at 617-945-1887, visit https://www.mccarthystoad.com/, or https://www.facebook.com/SomervilleSongwriterSessions or email SomervilleSongwriterSessions@gmail.com. Somerville Songwriter Sessions at McCarthy's presents contemporary folk singer/songwriters in concert on the second Sunday afternoon of each month. Each performer will do a solo set, followed by a round-robin with all three performers. McCarthy's features live music in a comfortable, listening room setting, and features a full menu and bar. Our 10/11 performers: Jim Infantino has been performing his own brand of off-kilter folk music since the '80s when he was an underage teen sneaking into Dave Van Ronk's open mic at The Speakeasy on Macdougal Street. His songs have been described as satirical, witty, sardonic, urbane, funny, heartbreaking, catchy, philosophical and razor sharp. Sometimes political, sometimes personal, sometimes abstract, his songs weave in the hint of humor when you expect sadness and tragedy when you expect levity. Since 1996 he has been performing both solo and with his band Jim's Big Ego, who describe themselves as "the greatest band in the history of recorded music." With the band he has released 7 full-length CDs adding to his 4 solo releases including his latest, 2025's Assemble Yourself. He is also a novelist, with his debut book The Wakeful Wanderer's Guide to New New England and Beyond winning the 2017 Wattys Newcomer's Award, and its sequel, The Wakeful Wanderer's Guide to Disillusionment, appearing in 2021. More on Jim at jiminfantino.co

title: Victorian Science and the Beyond: Ethereal Evening Tours
description: The spirit-world around this world of sense Floats like an atmosphere, and everywhere Wafts through these earthly mists and vapours dense A vital breath of more ethereal air. -From “Haunted Houses” by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow Scientific discovery – and the promise of glimpsing the world beyond our perception – captured the imaginations of 19th century Americans. Join Longfellow House-Washington’s Headquarters for a special evening of historic house tours exploring the intersections of Victorian scientific thought, the lure of the supernatural, and their echoes today. 50-minute tours will invite participants to examine the unknown as we consider the Longfellow family’s entanglements with forensics and phrenology, early views of outer space, the spiritualism movement, and their pioneering use of ether anesthesia. title: Fireside Chat with Libbie Grant
description: Join author Libbie Grant as she chats with Internet and Identity Scholar Judith Donath about her new novel THE ENDED WORLD! Libbie Grant's THE ENDED WORLD: A young woman’s vision over a Quebec lake sends her on a search to understand her relationship to the divine. While she spends years as a cloistered nun, a young boy struggles with his Mormon upbringing and, discovering the internet, grows up to design an AI entity that stuns him by appearing sentient. Embarking on their own separate road trips, these characters unite to face the scope of their responsibilities, their understanding of what’s holy, and the very question of what it is to be a human being. Steeped in philosophy, theology, and computer science, THE ENDED WORLD is a novel for our times. Judith Donath is a writer, designer and artist whose work focuses on the co-evolution of technology and society. She has published numerous articles about social media, AI, ethics and anonymity, and is the author of The Social Machine: Designs for Living Online (MIT Press). As the former director of the MIT Media Lab's Sociable Media Group, she and her students designed innovative interfaces for on-line communities; their art projects examining the future of identity, privacy and mediated life have been exhibited in museums and galleries worldwide. Currently, she is a faculty fellow at Harvard's Berkman Klein Center and is writing a book about technology, trust and deception.

description: Facing the Climate Crisis: Action and Love Stories About How We Face a Climate Crisis - And What We Love About Our Planet* These events bring together the delight of improvisation with the courageous vulnerability of people sharing their personal truth. The show’s emcee (called “the conductor”) facilitates brief, spontaneous conversations with volunteers from the audience who share their own feelings and experiences related to the show’s theme. After each conversation, the actors and musician immediately embody the key feelings and actions they heard, using movement, music, dialogue, and superb listening. All of it is improvised on the spot. During the course of a 75-minute show, True Story enacts about 6-8 stories. From this simple interaction, audience members feel validated, laugh, cry, get insights about their lives, and feel an expanded sense of community. You can share a moment from your life and see it performed, or just come to watch. More Info: https://truestorytheater.com/about-us/how-a-show-works/ Events noted with an * asterisk are supported in part by a grant from the Somerville Arts Council, a local commission supported by the City of Somerville. description: Join author Daisy Rockwell in conversation with professor and scholar Jared Green as they discuss her new novel ALICE SEES GHOSTS! Description of ALICE SEES GHOSTS: Alice Bloodshaw’s grandmother lies dying in their crumbling ancestral home. Family relationships are fraught, and worsened by the mercurial behavior of Alice’s mother. Then Alice, eccentric and attuned to the supernatural, is haunted by the specter of her grandfather. His cryptic message sends Alice and her Bengali psychiatrist fiancé, practical-minded Ronit, on a journey from New England to India and back again to unearth the long-buried truths that have choked and tormented the family. Bit by bit, Alice untangles the past to confront the legacy of aristocracy, secrecy, and colonialism in a quest to mend family ties and stop living as a ghost herself. Biography of Jared Green: Jared Green received both his A.M. and Ph.D. from Brown University. His scholarly essays and reviews on Modernist literature, visual culture, and early cinema have been published internationally. He is also a fiction writer and experimental literary performer and has published poetry, prose poetry, children's fiction, and screenplays. He is currently a professor of English at Stonehill College, as well as the Director of their Digital Humanities Program.

title: MOON COUNTRY: Contemporary Korean Poetry in Translation
description: Join Black Ocean and the Woodberry Poetry Room for an evening of readings and conversation celebrating the Moon Country Korean Poetry series, which brings contemporary Korean poetry into English translation. The program will explore the poems themselves as well as the intimate, collaborative work of carrying voice, image, rhythm, and cultural context across languages. Through readings and discussion, the participants will offer a glimpse into the choices, discoveries, and productive tensions that shape poetry in translation. The evening will be moderated by Black Ocean founder and publisher Janaka Stucky , with readings by Spencer Lee-Lenfield , Mattho Mandersloot , and Shin Hae-uk . IN-PERSON ATTENDANCE: Woodberry Poetry Room, Lamont Library, Harvard University. Free and open to the public. Spencer Lee-Lenfield is a translator and scholar of Korean literature and an Assistant Professor of Comparative Literature at Harvard University, where he teaches translation studies and researches Korean-English literary translation. His translation of Shin Hae-uk’s Biologicity , published by Black Ocean, was nominated for the 2025 Lucien Stryk Asian Translation Prize. His translations and writing have appeared in The Kenyon Review, Guernica, New England Review, The Yale Review , and The New York Review of Books . Mattho Mandersloot is a literary translator working from Korean into English and Dutch. A former taekwondo athlete, he earned a BA in classics from King’s College London, an MA in translation from the School of Oriental and African Studies and an MSt in Korean studies from Oxford. Among others, he has translated bestselling authors Cho Nam-joo and Sang Young Park. He has led several poetry translation workshops at the Poetry Translation Centre in London, and in 2020, he was awarded The Korea Times’ 51st Modern Korean Literature Translation Award for poetry. title: Screening of Presence
description: Join us for a midday screening exploring how public life has been staged, recorded, and remembered on screen. Presence is a film installation by Jingrong Zhang, supported by the Council for the Arts at MIT (CAMIT). Drawing on archival and cinematic footage across cultures and historical periods, the work assembles a "global supercut" of public gatherings: moments of solitude, chance encounters, street life, and collective assembly. As the montage builds from isolated figures to dense crowds, it invites viewers to consider how strangers come together in public space, and how those moments of shared presence have been captured on screen across a century of image-making. Every crowd on screen was once as present as we are now.

We'll be offering "big talk" conversation prompts to get you started, and we'll have lots of structure to make sure that you actually talk to people and that it's not awkward. Not feeling like answering a particular question? No worries, we'll have plenty to choose from, like, "When are you the happiest?" and, "If you were going to become close friends with me, what would I need to know about you?"

title: Walk to End Alzheimer's - Greater Boston
description: The Alzheimer's Association invites the community to join the Greater Boston Walk to End Alzheimer's on October 25, 2026, at DCR Richard McKinnon Park in Cambridge. The Walk is the world's largest event dedicated to raising awareness and funds for Alzheimer's care, support, and research. More than 7 million Americans are living with Alzheimer's, and nearly 12 million family members and friends provide unpaid care for loved ones living with the disease. Funds raised through the Walk help the Alzheimer's Association advance critical research efforts while providing free support, education, and resources to families facing Alzheimer's and other dementias. The Greater Boston Walk brings together individuals, families, caregivers, community organizations, and corporate teams who are united in the fight against Alzheimer's and all other dementia. Participants of all ages are welcome and can register as individuals or as part of a team. As part of the event, participants are invited to take part in the Promise Garden ceremony, a moving tribute that honors those impacted by Alzheimer's and other dementias. Each flower in the Promise Garden represents a personal connection to the disease and serves as a powerful symbol of hope and determination. This year, the Walk to End Alzheimer's - Greater Boston is expected to have about 5,000 participants and participants are working together toward a fundraising goal of raising $2 million to support the Alzheimer's Association's mission. Those interested in joining the movement can register, donate, or learn more at act.alz.org/GreaterBoston.

title: A Closer Look at Charley Longfellow’s “Japan Room"
description: Charles Appleton Longfellow (1844–1893), the eldest son of poet Henry Wadsworth Longfellow and Frances Appleton Longfellow, was a globetrotter and avid collector. During his 20-month stay in Japan (1871–1873), he purchased and shipped home to Cambridge dozens of crates of artworks and decorative objects for himself, friends, and family. Upon his return in 1874, Charley transformed the sitting room at his family home into a “Japan Room” with the help of his cousin Alexander Wadsworth Longfellow (1854–1934). One of its most striking features was a ceiling decorated with more than 35 fan-shaped paintings arranged in a “scattered fan” pattern. Although Japanese art and decorative objects had entered U.S. markets by the mid-1870s, their availability and visibility varied considerably by city. Created in 1874, on the eve of the transformative 1876 Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia, the Japan Room represents an unusually early American domestic interior devoted to Japanese art and design. This lecture examines its remarkable ceiling of fan paintings, exploring their origins and arrangement and considering how this distinctive feature of the room reflects the ways Japanese art was displayed and experienced in nineteenth-century America. This research was supported by the Friends of the Longfellow House-Washington's Headquarters 2025 Art Research Fellowship Program. ————————————— Elizabeth K. Eder, Ph.D., is a museum scholar, educator, and researcher who has worked at the Smithsonian Institution for more than 20 years, including at the Smithsonian American Art Museum, the National Museum of Asian Art (formerly the Freer Gallery of Art and Arthur M. Sackler Gallery), and the Anacostia Community Museum. Her museum career has also included positions at the Walters Art Museum, the National Gallery of Art, and the American Alliance of Museums. Her research interests include nineteenth-century American art; Chinese, Japanese, and European artistic influences on American a

title: Multispecies Warfare in Palestine-Israel: A talk by Irus Braverman
description: Brook Farm Institute for Critical Studies welcomes Radcliffe scholar Irus Braverman as the next speaker in our ongoing public lecture series, Critical Interventions. Animals have long played important roles in human warfare. Drawing on ethnographic research and on her own experiences growing up in Palestine-Israel, Braverman will explore how nonhuman animals have become active participants in Israeli warfare and how warfare itself has been shaped by their presence. Introducing the concept of “multispecies warfare,” she will show that animals are not simply instruments of military violence, but that they also acquire political significance through animal welfare regulations, animal rights initiatives, property regimes, and environmental protections. Sheep seize territory through grazing, dogs become subjects of rescue and humanization, donkeys sustain mobility under siege, crocodiles operate as imagined security technologies, and camel movement becomes criminalized through conservation laws. Warfare, then, is enacted through both violence and care. By tracing unexpected connections between humans, animals, and war, Braverman will offer a new way of thinking about warfare itself: not as an exclusively human endeavor, but as a complex multispecies project that shapes political worlds.

title: VOCARIUM READING SERIES: Ariana Reines & Eileen Myles
description: On the eve of the 2026 Midterm Elections, the Poetry Room invites you to come together for a reading by two of the most fearless, visionary, and uncompromising poets writing in America today, Ariana Reines and Eileen Myles. Together, Myles and Reines will offer a night of unruliness, resilience, tenderness, ferocity, and possibility. This not-to-missed evening will be introduced by K. Prevallet , who will provide an invocation. In-Person Attendance: Carpenter Center for the Visual Arts auditorium, 24 Quincy Street, Cambridge, Mass. Free and open to the public. Online Attendance: Livestreaming available via the WPR YouTube Channel . Myles will read from Bird Watching and Their First Three Books of Poetry (Fonograf, 2026), a dynamic new volume gathering a never-before-published long poem, circa 1978, with the three books that launched their poetic life. Restless, intimate, raw, and wildly attentive, these early poems already signal the emergence of one of the defining forces in American poetry. Reines will read from The Rose (Graywolf, 2025) and other new work . Moving between erotic desire and spiritual longing, violence and tenderness, The Rose is a book of bodies—historical, mythical, intimate, political—and of the elemental forces that move through them. This reading will mark the 2nd Annual Fanny Howe Memorial Reading.

title: Saturday Revival with ‘Bob Bradshaw Band'
description: Toad Revival Series — Saturdays, 4–7 PM Every Saturday from 4 to 7, we rewind the clock and let the old sparks fly. The Toad Revival Series is our tribute to the bands that built this stage, note by note, night after night. It’s a laid-back, early evening show filled with familiar sounds, longtime favorites, and the spirit of a scene that never really faded—just waited for the right time to plug back in. These are the artists who gave Toad its heartbeat, returning for intimate, no-frills sets that remind us why we’re here. Think front-porch energy with barroom volume, old songs with new life, and a crowd that knows when to sing along. Come early. Stay as long as you like. This is Toad, the way it was—and still is.

title: Fireside Chat with Rim Battal and Liza Tripp
description: Join author Rim Battal and translator Liza Tripp as they discuss the English release of Battal's novel I'll Look Myself in the Eyes! In this autobiographical coming of age novel, 17-year-old Rim is caught smoking out her window in her home in Marrakesh, Morocco. This minor transgression unleashes the fury of her mother who flies into a rage and demands that Rim complete a gynecological test certifying her virginity. So begins a nuanced journey into the tangled web of a patriarchal society in which various generations of women seem to complicitly preserve the status quo. Ultimately, it is Rim who breaks the cycle of dysfunction, rebels against tradition, confronts betrayal from the women closest to her, and dares to be her true self.

title: Circus Up Annual Benefit Show
description: Circus Up Hosts 7th Annual Benefit Show Featuring Local and National Circus Artists and Dancers The nonprofit Circus Up is celebrating another year of using social circus to expand possibilities for youth with its annual benefit circus show Sunday, November 8th at Arts at the Armory in Somerville. The evening will feature local and national circus and dance performances, comedy, a circus scavenger hunt for kids as well as raffle prizes. This year performers include world-renowned clowns Jonatas Campelo and Liam Gundlach, and a new circus show created and performed entirely by our very own Circus Up staff! The event will be brilliantly lit up by Illuminus! Chef Asia Mei’s Moonshine 152 will cater the event. Circus Up offers inclusive, equitable access to circus education to Boston-area youth. It prompts its own youth community troupe, Kirkos, which features a team of remarkable circus artists age 7 to 16 from underserved communities. The troupe celebrates what it looks like to courageously learn, play, and create together. Kirkos performs bold and uplifting shows across Boston and beyond, from the Statehouse to street fairs and many festivals like the DSNI Multicultural festival. Founded by circus artist and educator Leah Abel, Circus Up is Boston’s only nonprofit working to make circus arts more equitable and inclusive. In 2025, Circus Up was named one of four Model Equity Organizations by the Boston Cultural Council. Circus Up is also the recipient of grants from the Mass Cultural Council, DJ Henry Foundation, Jason Mraz Foundation, and more. For more information, check out Circus Up’s (circusup.com) or write to us at info@CircusUp.com.

title: Kintsugi-Inspired Stud Earring Workshop
description: Join Tokyo-born artist and kintsugi practitioner, Sayako Hiroi to make one of a kind earrings for yourself or to gift just in time for the holiday! When: Wednesday, November 11, 2026 from 7pm-8pm Location: Green Tiger, Bow Market Fee: $60 and all materials are included for you to make one set of earrings. You have the option to create additional sets for $25 each. You will first choose your favorite pieces from Sayako's curated selection of sea glass, ceramic shards, and gemstones. Then attach earring findings to make your own pair of stud earrings. Inspired by kintsugi, the Japanese art of repairing broken pottery with gold, each piece celebrates the beauty of imperfection and repair. Studs sit close to the ear and don’t swing, making them easy to wear every day. This workshop does not use lacquer, but it draws on kintsugi’s design language to help you create an accessory that exists nowhere else. About Sayako Hiroi: Sayako Hiroi is a Tokyo-born artist and kintsugi practitioner based in Boston. She holds an MFA from the School of the Museum of Fine Arts at Tufts University, and her work has been exhibited internationally, including solo shows in Tokyo and Boston. Her achievements have earned recognition including a Vermont Studio Center fellowship and a fully funded residency at the Ox-Bow School of Art. Bridging traditional Japanese craftsmanship and contemporary art, Sayako’s practice centers on kintsugi, the art of mending broken ceramics with gold. Built on repair rather than replacement, kintsugi celebrates giving objects a second life and finding beauty in imperfection. Through workshops and public engagements, she shares this philosophy with new audiences, preserving Japanese tradition while inspiring a more thoughtful, sustainable way of caring for the things we own.

title: Hiawatha Performances and the Garden River First Nation
description: In August of 1900, several members of the Longfellow family travelled to Desbarats, Ontario, where they had been invited to attend the first performance of Henry Wadsworth Longfellow’s poem Hiawatha put on by members of the Garden River First Nation. These productions, which spread throughout Indigenous communities across Western Ontario and Northern Michigan in the years that followed, featured largely Native actors and were performed in the Anishinaabe language. Analyzing these Hiawatha performances offers a window to explore how Native people reappropriated Western representations to insist on the survival of their own peoples and traditions. This event will feature two talks about the August 1900 performance based on research done in the collections held by the Longfellow House-Washington’s Headquarters’ National Historic Site. The first, by Professor Karl Hele, will describe the context and circumstances of the performance. The second, by Professor Alan Corbiere, will look at the use of the Anishinaabe language in the performances and in the material created for the Longfellow family. Alan Corbiere, Bne wedoodemid (Ruffed Grouse clan), is an Anishinaabe from M'Chigeeng First Nation on Manitoulin Island. He is an assistant professor of history and Canada Research Chair in Indigenous History of North America at York University. His research focuses on Anishinaabe language, oral traditions, and material culture. He has published in the journals Museum Anthropology, the Algonquian Papers, and others, as well as in the edited collection Afterlives of Indigenous Archives: Essays in Honor of the Occom Circle. He has also served as the the Executive Director at the Ojibwe Cultural Foundation and the Anishinaabemowin Revitalization Program Coordinator at Lakeview School, both in M’Chigeeng First Nation.
