description: Celebrate the music of Latin America across genres from merengue to tango to bossa, and even with a dance party to end it all! All ages! From bossa to bachata, from ranchera to rumba, from Tejano to tango, the music of Latin America spans a wide variety of genres and cultural experiences. With musical roots in West & Central Africa, Spain, Portugal, and the Indigenous communities of Central & South America and the Caribbean islands, Latin music has a long and storied history — sometimes ugly, sometimes beautiful, and always worth learning more about. title: Community Care Through Scarwork
description: 🌿 Join us Sunday, November 15, from 2:30–4:30 PM for a tender, body-centered workshop exploring Scarwork, gender-affirming care, and the healing that can unfold when we care for ourselves and one another. 🤗✨ 🫶 Led by Jeff Bramhall of Just Breathe Manual Therapy, this hands-on workshop is designed for trans* and gender-expansive folks who have undergone gender-affirming top surgery, as well as the people who support and care for them. 💗 Surgery takes a physical, mental, and emotional toll on the body, and healing continues long after the initial recovery period. Scars may hold areas of pain, numbness, altered sensation, or restriction, while access to ongoing, affirming aftercare can be limited. 🌱 Scarwork offers a gentle, intuitive approach to supporting healing. Rather than treating scar tissue as something to erase or fix, Scarwork invites us to meet it with curiosity, patience, and care. Through calm, attentive touch, this practice aims to support the integration of scar tissue with the surrounding tissues, potentially improving mobility, comfort, and connection with the body. 🫀 🤲 Together, we’ll explore: An introduction to scar tissue and the background and principles of Scarwork A demonstration of how Scarwork is practiced Introductory, hands-on techniques using gentle, listening touch Time to practice these techniques with a peer or partner through two mini-sessions 🪷 No prior experience with hands-on bodywork is necessary, only humility, curiosity, and a desire to be of service. This participatory workshop will intentionally cultivate a space grounded in consent, respect, and compassion, where each attendee can both receive and practice care with a peer. 🩷 Our goal is to build skills for sharing Scarwork as a free, community-based care practice, empowering participants to offer support to others in their communities and guide caregivers in providing gentle, attentive touch. This workshop is an introduction to community care, not professional training or prepa

description: Directed by Sofia Coppola, 2006. A fourteen-year-old girl leaves her home, her country and her puppy behind to marry a man she has never met. Twenty years later, she is the most despised woman in France. Sofia Coppola’s Marie Antoinette explores the rigid social structure and wild excesses of Versailles on the eve of the French Revolution. The film’s setting, shot on location, is extravagant, immense and overwhelming. The characters often seem to be swallowed up by the very architecture and landscape over which they rule. Casting actors known for comedy—Steve Coogan, Rose Byrne, Jason Schwartzman—highlights the understated humor running through a film that is fully aware of aristocratic absurdity without ever quite making it a punchline. title: Rubies
description: Rubies is a new, intimate collection of stunning minerals, gemstones, and jewelry on display in the Earth & Planetary Sciences Gallery. Ruby, the red variety of the mineral corundum, owes its vibrant color to trace amounts of chromium in its crystal structure. This element also gives many rubies a striking fluorescence, glowing bright crimson under ultraviolet light. Ruby’s internal world—its inclusions, growth zoning, and rutile “silk” needles—records its geological journey and can reveal its origin, making ruby a gemstone of extraordinary beauty and a rich source of scientific insight. title: Collecting Wonders: Tomorrow’s Discoveries
description: When you imagine a museum, you might picture cases of artifacts. But the objects on display at the Harvard Museum of Natural History are a tiny percentage of the total collections. Behind the scenes, experts care for 26 million specimens. These objects form the basis for studying life on Earth. They are records of the planet from different times and places. Objects span billions of years and come from every continent, ocean, and beyond. They are stone and bone, plant and animal, feather and fossil. Since the early days of Harvard University, collections have been central to teaching and research. People continue to study these collections and uncover knowledge. Come explore some treasures of the collection! Explore historic specimens presented to mark the 250th Anniversary of the United States Declaration of Independence on June 27. Check museum's website for closure dates.

Take a guess, then search for specific objects across our four museums—the Harvard Museum of Natural History, the Peabody Museum of Archaeology & Ethnology, the Harvard Museum of the Ancient Near East, and the Collection of Historical Scientific Instruments—to check your answers. title: Public Research Talk: Transcendentalism, Memorialization, and Harvard's Slavery History
description: Registration is required. Please register to attend in person . Please register to attend on Zoom . A house in Concord, Massachusetts, associated with one of the four founding benefactors of Harvard Medical School is currently threatened by a state transportation project. The house also occupies an unexpected place in the history of American Transcendentalism: Henry David Thoreau was the first to investigate its owner’s enslavement of Brister Freeman, one of the “former inhabitants” of Walden Woods who preceded Thoreau there. In addition to providing the stolen labor that helped establish an institutional leader in countless global health initiatives, Freeman also protested immoral poll taxes decades before Thoreau made tax resistance central to American political thought. This lecture argues that Harvard's ongoing reconstruction of its slavery "entanglements" (the university’s term) continues a distinctly Transcendentalist project of recovering obscured histories like Freeman’s by allowing conscience, rather than institutional convenience or financial considerations, to shape public memory. By tracing the intertwined histories of the endangered house, Harvard, slavery, and the Black moral tradition that culminated in American Transcendentalism, the lecture asks what meaningful acknowledgment and repair might look like today. Elise Lemire is Professor Emerit of English and Global Literatures at Purchase College, SUNY. Her research focuses on race, memory, and memorialization in the northeastern United States, with particular attention to Concord, Massachusetts, the shared birthplace of the nation and Henry David Thoreau. Lemire is the author of "Miscegenation": Making Race in America (2002), Black Walden: Slavery and Its Aftermath in Concord, Massachusetts (2009), and Battleground Vietnam: The 1971 March on Lexington, Concord, and Boston (2021), all published by the University of Pennsylvania Press. title: Richard P. Stanley Seminar in Combinatorics
description: Speaker: Hung-Hsun Yu (Princeton University) Title: The Erdős distinct distances problem in R^3 Abstract: In 1946, Erdős proposed the distinct distances problem: what is the least number of distances a set of N points in R^d spans? He computed that integer grids give an upper bound of O(N/(log N)^(1/2)) for d=2 and N^(2/d) for d at least 3. For d=2, a nearly matching lower bound cN/log N was obtained much later in 2010 by Guth and Katz, who introduced influential tools such as polynomial partitioning. In this talk, I will outline their proof and the extra twists needed to prove a lower bound of N^(2/3-o(1)) for d=3. Time permitting, I will briefly talk about the recent resolution of the distinct distances problem for d>=3 by OpenAI. This is based on joint work with Jonathan Tidor and Dmitrii Zakharov.

title: Hindu View of Life Lecture: Special Dispensations, Sublime Realities: Keshab Chandra Sen and the Comparative Impulse in the Nineteenth Century
description: Registration required. Please register to attend in person . Please register to attend on Zoom . Radhakrishnan’s lectures on Hindu views of life 100 years ago emphasize how the world then, after a devastating world war, was witnessing an interchange of thought between religions through the mingling of populations. Furthermore, the spirit of the age and the need of the hour determined the emphasis in each religion. This lecture will explore how interchange of thought between religions flourished in certain circles in nineteenth-century India, through an examination of the thought and major works of Keshab Chandra Sen (1838-1884), a Bengali philosopher of religion and social reformer who pioneered a range of comparative religious projects. Through an examination of his compilations of excerpts from a diversity of religious texts as well as his relationship to religions outside of Hinduism, Sen serves as a major precursor to Radhakrishnan’s contributions to modern and contemporary views on religion in the twentieth century. NEILESH BOSE is Professor and Graduate Advisor in History at the University of Victoria. His research focuses on modern South Asia, the British Empire, decolonization, migration, religion, performance, and global history. He is the author of Recasting the Region: Language, Culture, and Islam in Colonial Bengal and Chips from a Calcutta Workshop: Comparative Religion in Nineteenth Century India .

title: Uzbekistan, China, and the Green Transition: Rethinking Development in the Global South
description: How is Uzbekistan navigating economic liberalization and the green transition as China’s role in its industrial development expands? The talk examines the forces shaping this transformation, focusing on automotive production, electric vehicles, and renewable energy. It frames Uzbekistan’s economic doctrine as a form of postcolonial liberalism: an effort to overcome North–South hierarchies by reshaping, rather than rejecting, liberal globalization. It considers how partnerships with China and other Global South economies fit this vision, amid growing protectionist and illiberal currents in the West.

title: Richard P. Stanley Seminar in Combinatorics
description: Speaker: Greg Kuperberg (UC Davis) Title: My journey with the alternating sign matrix theorem Abstract: I will talk about the alternating sign matrix theorem and its proof from the point of view of my own experience with it: what led me to this problem, what I was thinking while working on it, and how I interpret the aftermath. Key elements include round enumerations in combinatorics, bijective versus algebraic proofs, Kasteleyn's theorem versus the Yang-Baxter equation, and factor exhaustion as a method to evaluate determinants. I will also discuss the sequel, symmetry classes of alternating sign matrices.

title: History of Now Lectures Series - Reluctant Neighbors: History of Jews in Palestine and the Levant, 1700-1850
description: History at MIT invites you to join us on Monday, November 16th at 5 pm in E51-095 for the third lecture in the History of Now series, featuring Orit Bashkin, the Mabel Greene Myers Professor of Modern Middle Eastern History and Director of Graduate Studies, Modern Fields at the University of Chicago. Her talk is titled "Reluctant Neighbors: History of Jews in Palestine and the Levant, 1700-1850." Orit Bashkin Mabel Greene Myers Professor of Modern Middle Eastern History Director of Graduate Studies, Modern Fields University of Chicago Monday, November 16, 2026 5-6:30 pm MIT Building E51, Room 095 Public Lectures Dates November 16 Reluctant Neighbors: History of Jews in Palestine and the Levant, 1700-1850 November 19 A Different Critique: MENA Jewish Approaches to Zionism and Imperialism, 1830-1948 About Orit Bashkin Orit Bashkin is a historian who works on the intellectual, social, and cultural history of the modern Middle East. She got her Ph.D. from Princeton University (2004), writing a thesis on Iraqi intellectual history under the supervision of Professors Robert Tignor and Samah Selim, and her BA (1995) and MA (1999) from Tel Aviv University. Since her graduation, she has been working as a professor of modern Middle Eastern history in the Department of Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations at the University of Chicago. Her publications deal with Iraqi history, the history of Iraqi Jews, the Arab cultural revival movement (the nahda) in the late 19th century, and the connections between modern Arab history and Arabic literature. Her current research project explores the lives of Iraqi Jews in Israel. To Attend All of these lectures are free and open to the public. More information on the lecture series is available here. For questions, please contact Professor Lerna Ekmekcioglu, Head of History at MIT, at lerna@mit.edu. We hope to see you there!

Tap dancing began as an answer to the horrors of colonial enslavement…with no musical instruments, Irish and West African slaves turned to their own feet to create rhythms and percussion while pulling movement and technique from traditional tribal and cultural dances. Sounds were initially made with wooden soles, then pennies and bottle caps, finally becoming the modern metal plates screwed to the ball and heel of the shoes. These dances made their way to minstrel and vaudeville shows, eventually transforming into the broadway and rhythm style tap dancing we know today. title: Saving Walden’s World’ to Screen in Brookline MA
description: What kind of world are we leaving for the next generation? In a time of mounting climate anxiety and geopolitical uncertainty, it is easy to feel that the system is failing. But while the headlines focus on extraction and conflict, there is a Plan B being engineered by communities in the places you'd least expect, and a Maine filmmaker went looking for it. Mothers Out Front Jamaica Plain, Mothers Out Front Brookline, Mothers Out Front Newton, Elders for Climate Action - Mass Chapter, and Climate Action Brookline are proud to present a special community screening of Saving Walden's World on Monday, November 16, 2026, at 7:00 PM, at the Coolidge Corner Theatre, 290 Harvard St, Brookline, Massachusetts. This film follows Jim Merkel's personal journey from a former military engineer to a father raising his son, Walden, on an off-grid homestead in Maine. Jim traveled to Kerala, Cuba, and Slovenia to investigate how communities there have achieved genuine stability, by prioritizing women's literacy, healthcare, and reproductive freedom, and what that means for the rest of us. Why attend? This isn't just a movie. It is a blueprint for a livable future. Recently accepted for national distribution on PBS via NETA, this Brookline screening is a rare chance for our community to engage with these solutions before they reach a national audience. Sliding scale ticketing. Seating is limited to 143, so save your seat by registering here. Donations towards the film's global impact campaign are certainly welcome. Q&A with director Jim Merkel will follow the screening. title: The Bowery Presents Liana Flores
description: The Bowery Presents Liana Flores Get Your Tickets! Doors open at 7:00 PM Show begins at 8:00 PM Liana Flores Biog “This record is the story of the country girl moving to the city,” Liana Flores says. “It’s bossa nova meets pop, inspired by the people, relationships and glamour of city life.” Since the release of her acclaimed 2024 debut album Flower of the soul, British-Brazilian singer-songwriter Liana Flores has been at the forefront of a bossa nova revival. Drawing on the ‘60s sound of genre pioneers like Joao Gilberto alongside pop songwriting, Flores combines the dual aspects of her cultural heritage to create an emotive sound. Following extensive tour dates across North America, Asia and Europe, Flores now returns with a new EP, And so it goes…, that expands her palette to encompass the playful and ebullient experiences of moving from her rural hometown in Norfolk to St. Andrews before coming to London. The result is a six track collection that shifts between finger-picked guitar and gossamer bossa vocals of “So it goes” to the upbeat funk inflections of the heavy-grooving love song “So mysterious”, the Carole King-influenced folk storytelling of “Here to stay,” and the sprightly, glittering pop melodies of “Silvershoes.” “These songs were informed by my experiences living in the city and touring for the first time. I grew up and studied in small towns with nature in my surroundings, so that’s what came naturally in terms of lyrics. With So it goes, the lyrics are more centred on human connection, and I wanted to explore a part of my identity that’s more playful and matter-of-fact. I also wanted to challenge myself to write songs with strong melodies that would be fun to sing or to get ready to.” Raised by an immigrant Brazilian mother and British father in East Anglia, Flores first began learning music while listening to ‘80s and ‘90s bossa nova artists like Bebel Gilberto and Leila Pinheiro alongside Top 40 pop radio. title: Jerry Bergonzi Quartet
description: $15 @ the door / $10 students / 8:30 start / 8pm doors / seated Jerry Bergonzi , Tenor Saxophone Luther Gray , Drums Plamen Karadonev, Piano Sean Farias, Bass Special Guest , Trumpet A fine, high-powered tenor saxophonist with a tone influenced by John Coltrane, a mastery of chord changes, and a strong musical imagination, Jerry Bergonzi has long had an underground following in the Boston area. He started on clarinet when he was eight, switching to alto at 12, and finally to tenor two years later. Bergonzi was inspired early on by Sonny Rollins, Coltrane, and Hank Mobley. He attended Lowell University and then after graduation played electric bass in local bands behind singers and strippers, saving up enough money to move to New York in 1972. After struggling in the Big Apple for seven years and gaining some recognition as a member of Two Generations of Brubeck and of the Dave Brubeck Quartet (with whom he appeared on several Concord albums during 1979-1981), Bergonzi moved back to Boston in 1981, where he developed a strong career both as a tenorman and as an educator. He has since led several groups (including two called Con Brio and Gonz) and recorded for the Plug, Not Fat, Red, and Blue Note labels. — By Scott Yanow, AllMusic Continuing Every Monday at 8:30pm Lineup subject to change

title: The Fringe
description: $15 @ the door / $10 students / 10pm doors / 10:30 start / seated The Fringe originally formed back in 1971 by tenor-saxophonist George Garzone , bassist Richard Appleman, and drummer Bob Gullotti as an outlet for their free jazz improvisations, The Fringe have entertained and enlightened Boston area jazz audiences for over 50 years. Bassist Appleman left the band in 1985 to become Chairman of the Bass Department at Berklee College and was replaced by veteran bassist John Lockwood . Bob Gullotti passed away in 2020 and is remembered as one of the greatest jazz drummers of his generation. Francisco Mela, now on drums, graciously fills the space Bob left behind. Along with their impressive tenure with The Fringe, Garzone, Lockwood, and Mela are in great demand as session players and have played with many of the greats of contemporary jazz. Along with keeping up with a busy performance schedule, each of them are well-respected educators helping to inspire the jazz musicians of tomorrow. title: Collecting Wonders: Tomorrow’s Discoveries
description: When you imagine a museum, you might picture cases of artifacts. But the objects on display at the Harvard Museum of Natural History are a tiny percentage of the total collections. Behind the scenes, experts care for 26 million specimens. These objects form the basis for studying life on Earth. They are records of the planet from different times and places. Objects span billions of years and come from every continent, ocean, and beyond. They are stone and bone, plant and animal, feather and fossil. Since the early days of Harvard University, collections have been central to teaching and research. People continue to study these collections and uncover knowledge. Come explore some treasures of the collection! Explore historic specimens presented to mark the 250th Anniversary of the United States Declaration of Independence on June 27. Check museum's website for closure dates.

title: Pop Quiz: 1776

Would Harvard students in 1776 have known about the things we see and do today? Take a guess, then search for specific objects across our four museums—the Harvard Museum of Natural History, the Peabody Museum of Archaeology & Ethnology, the Harvard Museum of the Ancient Near East, and the Collection of Historical Scientific Instruments—to check your answers. title: Rubies
description: Rubies is a new, intimate collection of stunning minerals, gemstones, and jewelry on display in the Earth & Planetary Sciences Gallery. Ruby, the red variety of the mineral corundum, owes its vibrant color to trace amounts of chromium in its crystal structure. This element also gives many rubies a striking fluorescence, glowing bright crimson under ultraviolet light. Ruby’s internal world—its inclusions, growth zoning, and rutile “silk” needles—records its geological journey and can reveal its origin, making ruby a gemstone of extraordinary beauty and a rich source of scientific insight. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? I am a dance artist, teacher and performer as well as a clinical social worker. Join members of our Straus Center staff for an informal monthly conversation about their work treating objects in our collections. Taking place just outside the Straus Center in the Lightbox Gallery, this presentation will give you the chance to get up close and hands-on with a selection of tools and materials used by conservation staff. In this session, Kate Smith , senior conservator of paintings and head of the paintings lab, will talk about various philosophical approaches to restoring loss in paintings. The Straus Center for Conservation and Technical Studies is a world leader in fine arts conservation, research, and training. The center’s laboratories are where conservation, conservation science, and curatorial practice intersect, coming together to enrich the understanding of and care for the approximately 250,000 objects in the Harvard Art Museums collections.

title: Online Seminar On Undergraduate Mathematics Education
description: Speaker: Alice Mark (Vanderbilt University) Title: Reframing “buy-in” during a phased adoption of course coordination Abstract: One of the major sticking points for departments thinking of coordinating their courses is buy-in from faculty. Will coordination mean that certain people just don’t teach that course? Do people just have to get on board, like it or not? Who has a say, and how? Do some faculty just get to opt out of the whole endeavor? Perhaps most importantly, how do we remain in collegial dialogue when we’ve decided to do this but don’t agree on all aspects of implementation? This session will not answer these questions. Rather, it will provide the opportunity to unpack them and brainstorm strategies relevant to your own course coordination project. Zoom link: https://cornell.zoom.us/j/92415199317 Zoom Link Password: olsume For more information on OLSUME: https://olsume.org/

title: Blind Tasting at Bonde Wine Shop
description: What happens when you take the label, the grape, the region, and the price, out of the equation? Every Tuesday at Maison at Bonde, we invite you to trust your palate with our Blind Tasting Flight. You choose the color and the body you feel like drinking. We choose the wines. Three wines are served blind, without labels or clues, giving you the chance to focus entirely on what is in the glass: color, aromas, texture, acidity, fruit, structure…and your own instincts. There are no wrong answers, and no wine knowledge is required. The idea is simply to taste first and think second, and perhaps discover how much our expectations influence what we believe we like. After tasting, we reveal the wines and talk about what you experienced. Every Tuesday · 12 PM to 9 PM · No Reservations, just show up! 3 wines · 6 oz total · $19 Come alone, bring a friend, challenge each other, and see whose palate gets closest. Sometimes the best way to discover wine is not knowing what you're drinking. Who are we? We're Bonde Fine Wine Shop and Tasting Bar . We're a small wine shop in Harvard Square that specializes in eco-responsible wines, primarily from the US, and neo-artisan accessories. We also are a tasting bar, where you can come and sit for a flight of wines with food anytime we are open. Follow us on Instagram , and sign up for our once-weekly newsletter on our website .

title: The 2026 Midterms: What Voters Told Us with Adam Geller
description: What did the 2026 midterm elections reveal about the American electorate—and what do the results mean for the future of both parties? Join the Institute of Politics for a timely conversation with Adam Geller, CEO of National Research Inc. and a leading Republican pollster. As part of the bipartisan polling team behind The Wall Street Journal poll, Geller brings decades of experience analyzing voter behavior and advising campaigns at the presidential, congressional, and gubernatorial levels. Drawing on his work in battleground states and his expertise in polling and focus groups, Geller will unpack the forces that shaped the midterm results, what voters’ choices reveal about the national political mood, and how the outcomes may reshape party strategy, messaging, and the road to the next election. Lunch will be served. NOTE: This event will be in Boylston Hall, Ticknor Lounge

title: Provably Secure: Math Against Superintelligent Hackers
description: Worry is growing around AI agents escaping containment and acting against the interests of the organizations that built them. The latest LLMs are also finding cybersecurity vulnerabilities in important software at an alarming pace. Against this backdrop, join the Social and Ethical Responsibilities of Computing on November 17 for a panel discussion exploring whether mathematical proofs could work to thwart superintelligent cyberattackers. Bringing together experts from academia, government, and industry, the conversation will survey an old computer-science technique with new promise: formal verification, mathematical proof about the behavior of programs. Can such proofs be applied to important computing infrastructure, to guarantee agent containment and find all security bugs of certain kinds, future-proofing against more-powerful LLMs? The panel will be moderated by Adam Chlipala, Arthur J. Conner (1888) Professor of Computer Science at MIT, and will feature Byron Cook, vice president and distinguished scientist at Amazon Web Services; Noah Evans, principal member of technical staff at Draper; and Armando Solar-Lezama, Distinguished Professor of Computing at MIT.

description: Join us at the Opening Reception for the new art exhibition by Natasha Boutureira. Natasha Boutureira is a Caracas born, Miami raised visual artist, whose work represents her experience as living between cultures. Artist Statement: My paintings explore the space I exist in as a Venezuelan immigrant, a third borderland shaped by overlapping cultures, memories, and experiences. I paint objects my family brought from Venezuela, using photographs of my parents’ apartment that feel familiar yet foreign, inherited rather than remembered. Through digital manipulation, CMYK color, distortion, and language drawn from my upbringing as a Venezuelan in Miami, I merge secondhand memories with lived experience. My work becomes a way of actively constructing the memories I cannot directly recall, exploring belonging as something constantly being made. @Bouuhaus

title: Blues Dance Lesson and Social - Bluesy Tuesy
description: Bluesy Tuesy is a friendly weekly social partner dance held on Tuesdays in Magoun Square at NESFA (504 Medford St, Somerville, MA). Partners not required. Come solo, with dance partners, or friends! Blues is a dance form that allows for a great diversity of expression, with a broad vocabulary. It developed along with swing dance in African-American communities as a blend of African and European dance styles. The dance has a heavy focus on partner connection, and connection to the ground with weight and momentum. There is a definite "pulse" as the dancer sinks in with each beat. It is a tonic for the soul. Through it, we can connect to the past, the present, and each other. The 4th Tuesday of every month is a Fusion dance instead of a Blues dance. Fusion is also a partner dance that combines aspects from assorted partner dances and applies them in a freeform style. Each evening includes a 1 hour beginner-friendly lesson before the social dance. (7:30p - 8:30p) Lesson (8:30p - at least 10p) Social Dance Admission is sliding scale, $5-$20 cash only For more information, and a week-to-week details, check out our website and facebook pages. title: Pop Quiz: 1776
description: Step back into the 18th century and put your detective skills to the test! Pop Quiz: 1776 takes you on a four-museum adventure to uncover surprising ways that life at Harvard was both similar to and—or different from —today. Would Harvard students in 1776 have known about the things we see and do today? Take a guess, then search for specific objects across our four museums—the Harvard Museum of Natural History, the Peabody Museum of Archaeology & Ethnology, the Harvard Museum of the Ancient Near East, and the Collection of Historical Scientific Instruments—to check your answers. Pro tip: join us any Sunday–Friday 11:00 am–4:00 pm to access all four museums! Check museum's website for closure dates.

title: Collecting Wonders: Tomorrow’s Discoveries
description: When you imagine a museum, you might picture cases of artifacts. But the objects on display at the Harvard Museum of Natural History are a tiny percentage of the total collections. Behind the scenes, experts care for 26 million specimens. These objects form the basis for studying life on Earth. They are records of the planet from different times and places. Objects span billions of years and come from every continent, ocean, and beyond. They are stone and bone, plant and animal, feather and fossil. Since the early days of Harvard University, collections have been central to teaching and research. People continue to study these collections and uncover knowledge. Come explore some treasures of the collection! Explore historic specimens presented to mark the 250th Anniversary of the United States Declaration of Independence on June 27. Check museum's website for closure dates.

title: Rubies
description: Rubies is a new, intimate collection of stunning minerals, gemstones, and jewelry on display in the Earth & Planetary Sciences Gallery. Ruby, the red variety of the mineral corundum, owes its vibrant color to trace amounts of chromium in its crystal structure. This element also gives many rubies a striking fluorescence, glowing bright crimson under ultraviolet light. Ruby’s internal world—its inclusions, growth zoning, and rutile “silk” needles—records its geological journey and can reveal its origin, making ruby a gemstone of extraordinary beauty and a rich source of scientific insight. Check the museum's website for closure dates.

title: The Utility of the Future: Electrification, Innovation and the Energy Transition
description: Sumeet Singh, Chief Executive Officer of Pacific Gas and Electric Company, previously served as Executive Vice President (EVP), Operations and Chief Operating Officer of PG&E, responsible for the utility’s operations, including gas, electric and generation, as well as the safety, vegetation management, wildfire and emergency operations. Prior to that, he was the EVP, Chief Risk Officer (CRO) and Chief Safety Officer, overseeing the company's integrated workforce health and safety strategy, its safety culture, and management of both operational risks such as wildfires, nuclear, dams, natural gas, natural disasters and non-operational risks such as cybersecurity, pandemic and others. Singh has held other leadership roles within PG&E, including serving as the Senior Vice President, CRO, and Vice President, Asset Management and Community Wildfire Safety Program. Singh also served as Vice President of Portfolio Management & Engineering in PG&E's Gas Operations, responsible for planning, prioritizing and providing oversight of Gas Operations' portfolio of work, and as Vice President, Asset & Risk Management in PG&E's Gas Operations. He joined PG&E in 2000 as an engineer, and also worked in various natural gas distribution and transmission engineering roles, as well as in the Finance and Energy Procurement functions. In 2025, Singh won the Top Chief Operating Officer sponsored by the San Francisco Business Times. Singh holds a Bachelor's Degree in Civil and Environmental Engineering from the University of California, Berkeley; and a Master of Business Administration degree from UCLA Anderson School of Management. In 2024, he completed the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Nuclear Reactor Course for Utility Executives. He is a registered professional Civil Engineer in the State of California. Singh serves on the Boards of GTI Energy, American Gas Association (AGA), and Nuclear Energy Institute (NEI). MODERATOR: Nicola De Blasio, Research Associate, Harvard-China Project

title: Intermediate/Advanced Ballet with Dean Vollick
description: Class begins with a thorough set of exercises at the barre that last from 30 to 45 minutes. Centre practice follows, and may consist of a battement tendu exercise, a battement jeté exercise, a grand battement exercise, small and/or large adage, stationary turns, traveling turns, and petite and grand allegro enchaînement (small and big jumps). Classes are structured so that the dancer warms up their feet, legs, hips and upper body gradually. As class progresses there are more changes of weight and eventually, sudden changes of direction. Live music is provided by a pianist, that ranges from classical pieces to selections from ballet repertoire to improvisational contemporary music. Cost: $20 Single Class | $15.00 barre | 5-class package $90.00 *NEW* The Dance Complex requires ALL visitors to have a Membership, Guest Pass, or $5 Day Pass to access the building. Please register in studio with the class assistant Accepted Payments: Cash, Check, Venmo What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? Ballet originated in the Italian Renaissance courts around 1500 as large balls or spectacles that were performed by members of the royal court. The French king, Louis XIV, created the first academy and the positions, steps, and movements of the ballet were collected and codified. The spectacles began to be performed by artists that were trained in the academy, originally as part of an opera, and later as ballets that told a story through music, mime, and dance. Over the centuries ballet has influenced folk dance styles of many (mainly European) nations and, more recently, has been influenced by folk, modern, and contemporary forms of dance from all countries. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? I had a professional dance career that spanned more than twenty years and included company work in both ballet and contemporary companies as well as dancing, choreographing, and teaching as a freelance artist.

description: How to join: Check in at the Visitor Services desk; space is limited. Fee: This is a free event. Accessibility accommodations: If you would like to request accommodations for your visit, please contact Visitor Services at am_register@harvard.edu or 617-495-9400. For more details about accommodations at the museums, please see the Accessibility page. Join Ally Cirelli, curator of Alfonso Ossorio: Line and Lineage (October 23, 2026–April 11, 2027) at the Harvard Art Museums, and Danni Shen, curator of Knowledge Is Myth: Chimeric Continuities (October 1–December 13, 2026) at the Carpenter Center for the Visual Arts, for a multi-site tour of the two interconnected exhibitions. At the Harvard Art Museums exhibition, we will explore the experimental processes of modern artist Alfonso Ossorio and work by contemporary artists Enzo Camacho and Ami Lien that respond to his artistic legacy in the Philippines. Continuing to the Carpenter Center, we will view more works by Ossorio, Camacho, and Lien as well as other contemporary artists working with mythology. Throughout the tour, Cirelli and Shen will highlight the intergenerational connections made by these artists through material experimentation. Led by: Ally Cirelli , Cunningham Senior Curatorial Assistant for the Collection, Division of Modern and Contemporary Art, Harvard Art Museums Danni Shen , Senior Curatorial and Public Programs Assistant, Carpenter Center for the Visual Arts

title: Richard P. Stanley Seminar in Combinatorics
description: Speaker: Jim Propp (UMass Lowell and Radcliffe Institute) Title: Snake graphs and q-deformed real numbers Abstract: I'll present a statistical-mechanical construction of q-deformed real numbers [[x]]_q, inspired by the q-deformed rational numbers [x]_q of Morier-Genoud and Ovsienko. The new construction admits two equivalent formulations: one in terms of random filters in snake posets and the other in terms of random dimer covers of snake graphs. I'll begin with a combinatorial approach to Stern's diatomic series and the Calkin–Wilf bijection via finite snake graphs, and then construct q-deformed rational numbers by introducing an activity parameter q into the model. I extend from q-deformed rationals to q-deformed reals by passing from finite to infinite snake graphs; the main technical step is to show that the associated limiting probability measures are well defined. The resulting q-deformation [[x]]_q satisfies [[x]]_1 = x for all x>0. There's evidence that, wherever both [x]_q and [[x]]_q are defined, [[x]]_q = q [x]_q. For more details, see arXiv:2607.14332.

title: Lie Groups Seminar
description: Speaker: Shamgar Gurevich (University of Wisconsin-Madison) Title: A Look at Representations of SL(2,q) Via the Lens of Size: Motivations, Rank, Eta Correspondence. Abstract: Harmonic analysis studies functions on the real line by expanding them as sums of frequencies (exponentials) and analyzing how each term contributes to the whole. In many applications—such as speech recognition—only the low frequencies matter. Over the last fifty years, Roger Howe (Yale) has developed the philosophy that such “analysis by frequency” should apply far beyond the real line. In joint work with Roger, we have introduced an analogue of this theory for finite classical groups. A class function on a finite group can be expressed as a linear combination of irreducible characters, and we define a notion of “frequency” or “size” (which we call rank) for such objects. This provides a new way to analyze class functions on finite groups. For example, before our work, it was not even clear in what terms one could bound the values of irreducible characters on various group elements. In this talk, I will try to sell you on this approach through the first nontrivial example of the group SL(2,q) of 2×2 matrices with entries in the finite field Fq and determinant equal to one.

title: MIT Music Tech Speaker Series Presents: Mark Ethier
description: Tools for Musicians in the Age of AI: From iZotope to Berklee Music and technology have always co-evolved. Long before the synthesizer, innovations ranging from new tuning systems to the piano's sustain pedal haven’t just made music easier to produce — they’ve fundamentally changed what kind of music is possible to make. How will AI as an underlying technology fit into this history? Since I was an undergraduate at MIT, I’ve spent my career building tools for musicians and watching this interplay firsthand. Sometimes, new technology inspires the music itself, like how rhythmic delay helped inspire U2’s “Where the Streets Have No Name.” Other times, musicians drive the technology. At iZotope, our collaboration with BT on Stutter Edit took intricate audio effects that could require hours of studio editing and made them playable in real time onstage. I’ve also witnessed the impact of the democratization of music making. We helped build a path for musicians to launch careers from their bedrooms, but we also watched large-format studios close their doors. It’s too early to fully grasp how generative AI will impact creative possibilities and livelihoods, but I'll share some early signals from recent market research, including Berklee’s June 2026 report, In Sync: Music and Video 2026. Now, we’re entering a new phase: the democratization of tool building. With a quiet revolution of musicians vibe-coding their own tools, this story is far from over. In these moments of change, it’s often clear what is being lost. But we also have to wonder what new artistic expression becomes possible, and with the evolution of generative AI, question who gets to shape that change and benefit from it. Speaker Bio: Mark Ethier is an entrepreneur and innovator dedicated to empowering creativity. In 2001, after graduating from MIT with degrees in music and computer science, he cofounded iZotope. title: Good Refugees, Bad Refugees: Borders and Belonging in Southeast Europe
description: Who gets to be a “good” refugee, and who is cast as a threat? What determines whether displaced people are welcomed, tolerated, or turned away? Southeast Europe, historically a crossroads of migration, displacement, and contested national identities, offers a fascinating lens through which to examine these questions. Drawing on Dr. Mandic's forthcoming book, Bad Refugees: Geopolitics, Stigma and Forced Migration, this talk explores how nationality, ethnicity, geopolitical interests, and public narratives shape distinctions between “deserving” and “undeserving” refugees with particular attention to Southeast Europe.

description: Join us for an engaging evening with author Thomas Levenson as he discusses his new book, "A Pox on Fools: The True Believers, Grifters, and Cynics Who Convinced Us to Reject Vaccines," in conversation with MIT Museum Director Michael John Gorman. Since the advent of smallpox inoculation in the eighteenth century, the idea that a disease introduced to the body in some lesser, weakened form might prevent full-blown infection has been one of the greatest public health insights of the modern era, inspiring the invention of numerous vaccines and saving countless human lives. But, just as humanity acquired the superhuman ability to stop infectious disease in its tracks, some feared we had gone too far, leading to skepticism that has hijacked public health discourse today. In three sweeping essays written for our current moment of scientific mistrust, Thomas Levenson searches for the origins of the most common arguments against vaccines: that they are unnatural; that they are more dangerous than the illnesses they claim to prevent; and that they are an affront to freedom. Each arose from the earliest development of particular vaccines and the campaigns to distribute them. Even as the pattern repeats, Levenson reveals how innocent that skepticism initially was and, in each case, how very human fears and questions ultimately turned into something darker, where no truth would be enough to overcome the doubt. Copies of A Pox on Fools will be available for purchase and signing after the talk, courtesy of the MIT Press Bookstore. A limited number of free tickets are available for full-time students with ID. Please reach out to museumregadmin@mit.edu.

title: The Festivals of Drunkenness in the Temple of Mut
description: The Temple of Mut is an ancient Egyptian sanctuary dedicated to the mother goddess Mut. From the early New Kingdom (c. 15th century BCE) through the Roman era, this temple was the setting for several festivals of drunkenness. The archaeological remains of a columned hall at Mut’s temple indicate that these celebrations took place during the reign of Queen Hatshepsut (c. 1479–1459 BCE). These included the annual Drunkenness Festival and the major Theban ritual known as the Beautiful Feast of the Valley. In this lecture, Betsy Bryan examines how these festivals were celebrated at Mut and at other sites in ancient Egypt, highlighting their participants, rituals, and religious purposes. Free event parking is available with registration. Parking will be available starting at 5pm. Register by November 17 to receive parking registration instructions. Presented by the Harvard Museum of the Ancient Near East and the Harvard Museums of Science & Culture. Betsy M. Bryan is a historian and art historian of ancient Egypt and is a specialist in the New Kingdom (ca. 1600–1100 BCE). As professor emerita of Egyptian art and archaeology at Johns Hopkins University, she teaches in the Department of Near Eastern Studies. Her research interests include the organization and production of art and its social and cultural meanings, including performance and expressions of ritual. Bryan’s studies on the cult of Mut-Sekhmet are cited often. Her long-term field projects in the Temple of Mut in South Karnak (2001–2025) and in the Theban Tomb 92 of the Royal Butler Suemniut (1993–2001) on the West Bank of Luxor have extended her research into the Second Intermediate Period, c. 1700–1550 BCE. Bryan has curated art exhibitions for the Cleveland Museum of Art and the National Gallery of Art and has been both Curator and Director of the Johns Hopkins Archaeological Museum throughout her career at Johns Hopkins University.

No partner required. *NEW* The Dance Complex requires ALL visitors to have a Membership, Guest Pass, or $5 Day Pass to access the building. *Students who purchase a membership for the Dance Complex will get that $25 taken off their 10 class new student rate, bringing it down to $85. Linear Salsa is a hybrid dance that comes from Mambo (a Cuban style that was popularized in the 1950’s NYC Palladium). title: Live Blues & Roots Music Returns to Harvard Square: Wednesday Nights @ The Sea Hag Restaurant & Bar
description: The Sea Hag Restaurant & Bar and The Barrett Anderson Band are excited to announce a new weekly series, Blues & Roots Wednesdays , bringing live music back home to historic Harvard Square. “Cambridge, our fair city, and I share deep roots, and I’m thrilled to find a new musical home at The Sea Hag,” says Massachusetts-based singer/guitarist, Barrett Anderson. “Good music and good food are two of our most basic, fundamental needs,” he continues, “What great joy they give us. I am so happy to revel in that every Wednesday night with my dearest musical friends, and Kari and her incredible team at The Sea Hag. We go way back together, and I can’t imagine all the fun we have ahead.” Indeed, Anderson has strong connections to this scene. He remembers: “My first professional experience came when I was 15, backing up Muddy Waters’ band alums Pinetop Perkins and Bob Margolin at the original House of Blues on Winthrop Street. A few months after that I began busking, you’d often find me in Brattle Square or by the pit. This would have been mid/late 90s.” While still a teen, Anderson was a member of The Monster Mike Welch Band and Ronnie Earl & The Broadcasters (“Ronnie was my guitar hero. Then he was my teacher, then my boss. Now he’s my musical Father,” Anderson says), before eventually starting The Barrett Anderson Band in 2007. Anderson won a Boston Music Award (2013 Blues Artist of the Year), was on the Billboard charts (2020’s live album Hynoboogie spent 3 weeks on the Billboard Blues Album chart, peaking at #6), and was nominated for a Blues Music Award (2023 Band of the Year with Anthony Geraci & The Boston Blues All-Stars), all the while playing nationally, internationally, and locally in Cambridge and the greater Boston area. In addition to the musical roots, long-time locals may recognize Anderson from a decade serving tables and bartending at The Sea Hag’s sister establishment, Grendel’s Den, or from Abodeon, the mid-century modern shop started by his family. title: Jesse Gallagher + Steve Fell
description: $10 admission / 7pm / seated show Jesse Gallagher began living above the Lilypad in 2006, just a few blocks from where his grandfather grew up on Inman st. The band was featured in the New York Times, Rolling Stone, Spin & shared the stage with legendary acts Wu-Tang Clan , Toots & The Maytals , The Flaming Lips & Dr. Dog . Gallagher has a very active YouTube channel, making lots of psychedelic music videos and building a community of mindful listeners. @jessegallagher.tv Steve Fell is a guitarist, composer, and educator whose performing and recording career over the last twenty five years has reached across the boundaries of jazz, experimental, funk, free form improvisation, rock, electronic, reggae/calypso, hip-hop, psych, and many others. You’ll have the chance to talk to a lot of people - but nothing is forced. Every game is optional and built to give you an easy way in, not box you into awkward moments. 82% of past attendees said they made a connection they wanted to follow up on. “I felt more chemistry here in 90 minutes than I have on 90 apps.” – probably someone’s soulmate Nook's Themed cocktails from will keep things loose. We’ll guide you through the night - whether you’re an overthinker, a slow burner, or someone who thrives in organized chaos. And when you do meet someone you click with? Our signature calling card system lets you safely exchange info only if you both want to. No pressure, no awkward ask - just connection, on your terms. Afterward, linger in Bow Market's cozy corners Our last 10 events sold out in advance. This one will too! Come solo. Bring your single friends. Just don’t wait.

title: Rubies
description: Rubies is a new, intimate collection of stunning minerals, gemstones, and jewelry on display in the Earth & Planetary Sciences Gallery. Ruby, the red variety of the mineral corundum, owes its vibrant color to trace amounts of chromium in its crystal structure. This element also gives many rubies a striking fluorescence, glowing bright crimson under ultraviolet light. Ruby’s internal world—its inclusions, growth zoning, and rutile “silk” needles—records its geological journey and can reveal its origin, making ruby a gemstone of extraordinary beauty and a rich source of scientific insight. description: As AI reshapes the job market, workers are being asked to learn new skills. Yet evidence on which training programs lead to better jobs and higher wages remains mixed. Which pathways work—and how can they reach everyone who needs them? Join The EdRedesign Lab at Harvard Graduate School of Education, StriveTogether, and the Project on Workforce at Harvard for a conversation inspired by the newest episode of DREAM ON. In Atlanta, a hub of the data center boom, host Joe Posner meets workers whose careers were transformed by Per Scholas, a job training program with decades of evidence behind it. In this webinar, leaders will explore how AI is changing work and employer skill needs, which workforce pathways support economic mobility, how place-based partnerships can align education and training with local needs, and what it takes to scale proven approaches into national solutions.

title: Measurement on the Color Line: Scientific Instruments and the Making of Human Categories
description: "Everyone thinks they know what race is—but do they?" Ideas about racial categories and racial differences have been created and sustained through scientific, biological, anthropological, and medical practices. Measurement on the Color Line traces the development of present-day notions of race through the sciences, measurements, and data that produced them. From the eighteenth century to the present, scientific instruments have been used in studies that make claims about race and racial difference. Specific categories of people have been formed through acts of observation, measurement, and quantification. New sciences and technologies have been repeatedly applied to answer familiar questions about race. Since the end of the nineteenth century, some physicians and social scientists have offered a counter-narrative to challenge race-making measurements. Curated by Evelynn M. Hammonds, the Barbara Gutmann Rosenkrantz Professor of the History of Science and professor of African and African American Studies at Harvard, the exhibition draws directly from her co-authored book, with Bates College Professor Rebecca Herzing, The Nature of Difference: Sciences of Race in the United States from Jefferson to Genomics . Her research highlights how early scientific disciplines, including anthropology and medicine, sought physical justifications for social hierarchies. Measurement on the Color Line includes objects graciously lent from several institutions and individuals, including the Peabody Museum of Archaeology & Ethnology, the Dittrick Museum of Medical History at Case Western Reserve University, Archives and Special Collections at Amherst College, Ernst Mayr Library, Harvard Divinity School Library, Harvard Law School Library, Houghton Library, and artists Lucy Kim and Wendel White.

title: MIT MLK Scholar Presentation "Imitation of life: an exploration of the physical signatures of living systems" with Visiting Professor Michael Murrell
description: What makes living matter different from the inanimate world? Can life be understood through measurable physical quantities such as energy, heat, and entropy? In this talk, Dr. Murrell will explore how we can quantify the physical signatures of living systems and recreate aspects of their behavior using simple assemblies of biological molecules. By building systems that imitate life, we seek to understand the physical principles that make life possible.

title: What Happens When Technology Moves Faster Than Democratic Institutions Can Adapt? with Katie Harbath
description: Technology is transforming how campaigns communicate, how voters engage with politics, and how democratic institutions operate. But what happens when innovation moves faster than democracy can adapt? Join the Institute of Politics for the next installment of our Food for Thought series featuring Katie Harbath, author of Disrupting Politics: A Front Row Seat to the Collision of Technology and Democracy. Drawing on 25 years at the intersection of technology and politics—including a decade leading public policy at Facebook—Harbath will offer an insider’s perspective on how digital platforms have reshaped political campaigns, public discourse, and democratic participation. As artificial intelligence introduces a new set of opportunities and challenges ahead of the 2026 and 2028 elections, the conversation will examine how campaigns, technology companies, and policymakers are navigating this rapidly changing landscape, and what it will take to ensure democratic institutions can keep pace. Lunch will be served.

title: Harvard Pop Center Hybrid Social Demography Seminar: "Reproductive and maternal health in an era of policy upheaval”
description: The Hybrid Social Demography Seminar (SDS) series at the Harvard Center for Population and Development Studies provides a lively forum for scholars from across the university to discuss in-progress social scientific and population research. Social demography includes work that uses demographic methods to describe and explain the distribution of social goods across populations. The Social Demography Seminar series thus welcomes presentations on a wide variety of topics such as family, gender, race/ethnicity, population health — including mortality, morbidity, and functional health—inequality, im/migration, fertility, and the institutional arrangements that shape and respond to population processes. The long-term goal is to build a broad and multi-disciplinary community of social demographers at Harvard. The seminars are geared towards faculty, postdoctoral fellows, students, and those with other academic appointments (e.g., research scientist or associate). With the aim of disseminating scholarly research, The Harvard Center for Population and Development Studies hosts a diverse array of speakers. They do not represent or speak for the Center, the School, or the University, and hosting them does not imply endorsement of their views, organizations, or employers.

title: AI & Political Freedom
description: The present moment is defined by both the emergence of powerful artificial intelligence and a deepening crisis of liberal democracy. Must they be opposing forces? Theoretically, AI could strengthen civic participation, enable more effective governance, and expand citizens' capacity to hold powerful institutions to account. Yet, as we have seen, it can also place unprecedented pressure on democratic institutions, proliferate misinformation, and entrench corporate — and authoritarian — power in ways that prove difficult to reverse. Anthropic researcher and neuroscientist Matt Botvinick examines these possibilities in his new book, AI and Political Freedom: The Risk to Democracy and How to Respond, a subject he never imagined confronting when building his first neural network in the 1990s. Join Botvinick in conversation with Chinmayi Arun, director of the Yale Project on Information and Society, where Botvinick is also a fellow, to explore how AI might alter the balance of power between citizens and the governments that represent them, and which direction those scales might tip. Drawing on perspectives from technology, law, and global governance, the duo will consider the interconnected short- and long-term risks to political freedom, as well as opportunities to harnessing technology for greater public participation. As AI advances amid growing strains on democratic institutions, what will determine whether it becomes an instrument of liberation, subjugation, or both?

title: Social Media on Trial: Neuroscience, Addiction, and the Law
description: What does neuroscience tell us about social media addiction? In August 2026, Meta reached a landmark multistate settlement of up to $17.1 billion over allegations that Facebook and Instagram were designed to encourage compulsive use among children and adolescents. This raised questions about the relationship between neuroscience, technology, and corporate accountability. How do algorithmic feeds, intermittent rewards, and other engagement-maximizing features interact with the brain’s reward and learning systems? And to what extent can research on substance use disorders inform our understanding of problematic social media use? Join the Petrie-Flom Center, the Center for Law, Brain & Behavior, and the Neurotech Justice Accelerator at Mass General Brigham for a discussion with Stephanie Tabashneck, PsyD, JD, and Javier Mesa, PhD, JD, exploring the neuroscience of social media use and its implications for law and public policy. The conversation will examine adolescent brain development, the scientific debate surrounding behavioral addictions, and the challenges of establishing causation between social media use and mental health outcomes. Drawing on the recent Meta settlement and emerging litigation, the speakers will consider how courts and policymakers can distinguish scientific evidence from speculation, evaluate claims of addictive platform design, and develop evidence-informed approaches to protecting young people. This event will be recorded and shared at a later date.

description: Consciousness & Reality (C&R) 2026-27 Series Inaugural Colloquium Consciousness First: What Experience Tells Us About What Exists Thu, Nov 19th, 1 p.m. Eastern Time Online-only event. Zoom link: https://zoom.us/j/92871253560?pwd=I4rZU3N9vLUsB0a2uSXLK5sOW5pyBP.1 GIULIO TONONI Professor of Psychiatry & David P. White Chair in Sleep Medicine, University of Wisconsin–Madison Distinguished Professor in Consciousness Science, University of Wisconsin–Madison Director, Wisconsin Institute for Sleep and Consciousness Consciousness is all we have, the one thing whose existence is immediate and irrefutable, yet science’s standard extrinsic perspective has a hard time accounting for its presence and quality. Integrated Information Theory (IIT) reverses the order and takes the intrinsic perspective: it starts from the essential properties of experience and asks what a physical substrate must be like to account for them. The answer explains why consciousness depends on some brain regions but not others, why it fades in dreamless sleep, and why space feels extended and time flowing. It also implies that what truly exists is what exists for itself, and that AI can replicate what we do but not what we are. title: Small States in an Era of Great Power Competition
description: The intensification of great-power competition is a symptom of the deepening crisis of the US-led, rules-based international order. Imperfect as this order was, the post-Second World War period - and especially the post-Cold War era - provided an historically significant degree of stability, peace, economic integration and prosperity, particularly within the US sphere of influence. Its erosion is contributing to growing global disorder, with smaller states often paying the highest price. Georgia offers an early example. Russia’s invasion of Georgia in 2008, followed by the annexation of Crimea in 2014 and the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, illustrates how inadequate responses to aggression against smaller states can encourage further challenges to the international order. Yet small states are not necessarily passive victims of great-power competition. They can acquire strategic value by serving as providers of connectivity, offering strategically important goods, resources or infrastructure, and occupying geopolitical positions that make their independence valuable to major powers. The discussion will therefore examine how small states can preserve agency in an increasingly fragmented international system - and how they can transform geographical vulnerability into strategic relevance, making their sovereignty and security a shared interest rather than a matter of great-power indifference.

title: Applied Math Colloquium
description: Speaker: Nikhil Srivastava (University of California, Berkeley) Title: Zero Spacing of Polynomials, Free Probability, and Hyperbolicity Abstract: How does applying a differential operator to a real-rooted polynomial affect the spacing of its zeros? The answer to this question turns out to be related to seemingly faraway areas of mathematics --- free probability, information theory, and the theory of hyperbolic polynomials. I will explain this phenomenon in terms of some sharp entropic inequalities, where the log discriminant of a polynomial plays the role of the entropy and Hermite polynomials play the role of Gaussians. No prior background will be assumed. I will briefly discuss an alternate proof of one of the inequalities found by OpenAI in the context of the First Proof project, and report on the findings and current status of this project. Joint work with J. Garza-Vargas and Z. Stier.

title: History of Now Lectures Series - A Different Critique: MENA Jewish Approaches to Zionism and Imperialism, 1830-1948
description: History at MIT invites you to join us on Thursday, November 19th at 5 pm in E51-095 for the final lecture in the History of Now series, featuring Orit Bashkin, the Mabel Greene Myers Professor of Modern Middle Eastern History and Director of Graduate Studies, Modern Fields at the University of Chicago. Her talk is titled "A Different Critique: MENA Jewish Approaches to Zionism and Imperialism, 1830-1948." Orit Bashkin Mabel Greene Myers Professor of Modern Middle Eastern History Director of Graduate Studies, Modern Fields University of Chicago Thursday, November 19, 2026 5-6:30 pm MIT Building E51, Room 095 About Orit Bashkin Orit Bashkin is a historian who works on the intellectual, social, and cultural history of the modern Middle East. She got her Ph.D. from Princeton University (2004), writing a thesis on Iraqi intellectual history under the supervision of Professors Robert Tignor and Samah Selim, and her BA (1995) and MA (1999) from Tel Aviv University. Since her graduation, she has been working as a professor of modern Middle Eastern history in the Department of Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations at the University of Chicago. Her publications deal with Iraqi history, the history of Iraqi Jews, the Arab cultural revival movement (the nahda) in the late 19th century, and the connections between modern Arab history and Arabic literature. Her current research project explores the lives of Iraqi Jews in Israel. To Attend All of these lectures are free and open to the public. More information on the lecture series is available here. For questions, please contact Professor Lerna Ekmekcioglu, Head of History at MIT, at lerna@mit.edu. We hope to see you there!

title: Harvard Square French Fry & Pairings Food Tour
description: Harvard Square is famous for so much — Harvard University, eclectic bookshops, buskers, and a food scene that punches well above its weight. But here’s what most visitors don’t know: it’s also home to some of the best french fries in all of Massachusetts . Together with our guide Larom, a Harvard alum, we built an entire tour around that fact, and it’s become one of the most unique food experiences in Cambridge. On this 90-minute walking adventure, you’ll sample distinctly different styles of fries at three beloved Harvard Square spots — from classic hand-cut wedges to smoky BBQ fries to legendary sweet potato fries — each paired with a drink chosen specifically to bring out the flavors. We’ll try the original raspberry lime rickey , a refreshing peach lemonade , and a crazy ice cream frappe that has to be seen to be believed. All pairings are non-alcoholic, making this tour genuinely fun for the whole family. Along the way, your guide will walk you through the beloved cobblestone streets past Harvard Yard , the Widener Library , the quirky Harvard Lampoon building , and the storied Harvard Faculty Club — sharing the funny, fresh, and occasionally absurd stories that make this neighborhood unlike anywhere else in Boston. You’ll also hear the full saga of the French Fry Wars of the late 20th Century , a deliciously bizarre chapter of local food history that explains why Harvard Square’s fry scene is what it is today. This food tour is ideal for: Visitors to Boston looking for a memorable, off-the-beaten-path Cambridge experience Families with kids and teens who want something interactive and delicious Date nights — quirky, fun, and plenty of good food Birthday celebrations and small group outings Local students, grad students, alums, and neighbors who want to see a new side of Harvard!

title: Co-Adaptive—Ruth Mandl and Bobby Johnston
description: Co-Adaptive—Ruth Mandl and Bobby Johnston Part of the MIT Fall 2026 Architecture Lecture Series Presented with the Architecture and Urbanism Group CO₂ COAdaptive As our planet gets hotter, and more extreme weather events become the norm, CO Adaptive is positioning themselves as an unbuild, design and build practice: a new model that reunites designers and builders through collaboration in order to re-think our joint role in shaping the built environment; contending with architecture at the intersection of saving embodied carbon and reducing operational energy. As stewards of the existing material repository contained in our cities, CO Adaptive aims to increase the resilience and reusability of all that already surrounds us. Their talk will engage the breadth of the practice’s work—from adaptive reuse projects and high-efficiency retrofits to material salvage operations, remanufacturing, and design for disassembly. These projects yield a critical perspective on how buildings and materials re-engage in their next iteration of use, working towards a reality in which extractive and depleting habits are replaced by a circular library of abundance. CO Adaptive is an unbuild-design-build practice founded by Ruth Mandl and Bobby Johnston in 2011. Initially it was started as an architecture practice, focused on retrofitting existing building stock to create energy efficient, climate resilient and spatially beautiful environments. To have a greater impact on the process of taking old buildings apart—emphasizing deconstruction, and shaping attitudes about “waste”—CO Adaptive Building was established in 2021 and CO Adaptive Disassembly in 2026. The attention of all three intertwined practices is on converting existing buildings from a linear economy to a circular one. CO Adaptive’s work has received numerous awards and recognition, including winning the Architectural League’s Emerging Voices 2026, A|N’s 2025 Best of Practice Award, and the 2025 Trust for Governors Island Climat

title: The Life of George B. Schaller and the Future of Conservation
description: Field biologist and conservationist George B. Schaller is renowned for revolutionizing the study of wildlife by observing animals in their natural habitats. He has also been a powerful advocate for protecting wilderness and animal species across the globe. Born in 1933 in Berlin to an American mother and a German father in Berlin, Schaller spent his war‑torn childhood searching for peace among wild creatures. His efforts took him around the world to study Congo mountain gorillas, Himalayan snow leopards, Brazilian jaguars, Tibetan brown bears, and many others. Before Jane Goodall or Dian Fossey, Schaller revealed the rich emotional and social lives of these primates and predators. Drawing from her new book Homesick for a World Unknown: The Life of George B. Schaller (Penguin Press, 2026), Miriam Horn will trace his remarkable career. She will highlight his views on conservation and the path to survival he mapped for us all—challenging us to rethink our place in the natural world. Copies of Homesick for a World Unknown will be available for purchase after the program. Free event parking is available with registration. Register by November 18 to receive parking registration instructions. Miriam Horn is a bestselling author, environmental advocate, journalist, and filmmaker. Her previous books include Rebels in White Gloves , Earth: The Sequel (coauthor), and Rancher, Farmer, Fisherman . She produced two documentary films, with one premiering at Sundance. Before writing books, Horn worked at the Environmental Defense Fund and the U.S. Forest Service, and wrote for magazines and newspapers, including The New York Times. She lives in Colorado’s South San Juan Mountains.

She was a founding member of the Terpsichore Ensemble in Amherst, MA and taught tap classes in Amherst and Northampton, MA before moving to Boston. title: An Exploration of Scotch Whisky *In-Person*
description: It's been said that if whisky was invented in Ireland, it was perfected by the Scots. “Uisge beatha” is the Scottish Gaelic term for “water of life”, which has been shortened to whisky. With its first iteration made around 1000 years ago, the Scottish have taken the craft of whisky production to its highest level, leaving Scotch whisky in a class of its own. It remains the shining example of spirit production throughout the world, and in this class we'll be exploring, learning and tasting these fine whiskies. From the Scottish Highlands and Speyside, down to ocean battered shores of Islay and Campbelltown, we'll learn how climate, flora and tradition affect the flavor profiles of some of the best whisky on the planet. This dance form was introduced to the United States and Europe at the turn of the 20th century, but it was not widely performed or taught until the 1950s and 1960s, when the belly dance craze swept across the U.S. The American cabaret style of belly dance is rooted in the legacy passed down by notable American teachers and performers, who blended Middle Eastern influences with their own innovations and movement styles drawn from diverse dance backgrounds. title: AJ Lee & Blue Summit
description: AJ Lee & Blue Summit are an award-winning, energetic, charming, and technically jaw-dropping band quickly rising on the national roots music scene. Originally based in Santa Cruz, California, the group met as teenagers, picking and jamming together as kids at local bluegrass festivals until one day, they decided they would be a band. After almost a decade on the road, they have established themselves as one of the most exciting and dynamic groups in Bluegrass. The band is AJ Lee on mandolin, fiddler Jan Purat, Sullivan Tuttle on guitar, and Sean Newman on Bass. The band carries that youthful, festival-parking-lot energy with them still today, but at the same time there’s a genuine ease and confidence to their music making. Their critically acclaimed third studio album City Of Glass was released on Signature Sounds records in 2024. 2025 saw the release of a series of covers featuring guests such as Lindsay Lou, Trey Hensley, Ahn Phung and Kyle Tuttle called Cover to Cover V.1. Cover to Cover V1 explores the wide variety of musical interests and influences that have helped AJ Lee & Blue Summit develop their unique sound as a band. “Tear My Stillhouse Down”, featuring guest vocals from Bluegrass and Americana powerhouse Lindsay Lou, comes from one of AJ’s favorite singers and songwriters, Gillian Welch. The band pays tribute to their California roots with a steaming Bluegrass version of New Riders of the Purple Sages “Glendale Train” featuring Molly Tuttle and Golden Highway’s own Kyle Tuttle (no relation!). Sully Tuttle, Molly’s younger brother, takes the lead on the early jazz burner “Who Walks In (When I Walk Out)” which features inspiring guest appearances from Grammy Award winning guitarist Trey Hensley and renowned flutist Ahn Phung. AJ takes back the lead on a striking rendition of the country classic “Takes One to Know One”. The EP closes out with former member Scott Gates taking the lead on his country ballad style rendition of The Monkees class and Shrek famo

title: Tap Level 2
description: Carrying on the tradition of Boston Tap, established by Maureen Cosgrove in 1976, these classes focus on developing technique, rhythm and musicality. Prior tap experience is recommended for Level 2 (Intermediate). Classes are workshop format, typically 7-week sessions. Each class will build on the weeks before, but students may join at any time if space allows. Written notation for set warm-ups are available for those who are interested. New 7-week tap session 10/29-12/17 (no class 11/26) Cost: $20 single class | 7 week session $120 *NEW* The Dance Complex requires ALL visitors to have a Membership, Guest Pass, or $5 Day Pass to access the building. REGISTRATION: Email selapbailey@gmail.com Pre-registration required. Accepted Payments: Cash, Check, PayPal, Credit Card, Apple Pay (email selapbailey@gmail.com for payment information) What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? Tap is an American dance form in which rhythms are audibly tapped out on the floor. It has origins in slavery and the percussive dances of West African Juba dance and Irish step dancing. It developed through minstrel shows and vaudeville in the late 19th century and emerged along with jazz in the 20th century into the art form we know today. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? Sela has been a tap teacher since 2000, taking over Maureen Cosgrove’s Boston Tap classes at the Dance Complex in 2014. While at Smith College she studied in the Five College Dance Department, performing with the Celebrations Dance Company and the UMass University Dancers. She was a founding member of the Terpsichore Ensemble in Amherst, MA and taught tap classes in Amherst and Northampton, MA before moving to Boston. Sela teaches adult beginner and intermediate tap classes at the Dance Complex, and made her Dance Complex choreographic debut at the 2018 Spring Teaching Artists and Student Concert with students from the intermediate tap class.

description: The Mail, Wood & Bone and Objects in Motion live at the Lizard Lounge Nov 19th! Early Bird $12 (limited to First 20 Presale) $15/$20 door Doors 6:30 The Mail emerged from the vibrant music scene of Boston in 2016, born out of a shared passion for sonic experimentation and storytelling. Composed of members Jeremy Van Cleave, Joe Campbell, Nathaniel Diamond-Jones, Matt Hines, and Curtis Hartshorn, this ensemble quickly made waves with their distinct blend of folk rock and alternative influences. Driven by a mutual desire to carve out their own musical niche, The Mail’s sound is characterized by Jeremy’s introspective lyrics, Curtis’s unique drumming, Matt’s creative chord voicings, Joe’s deep bass pocket, and Nathaniel’s distinctive approach to fiddle. Together, they create a sonic landscape that is both emotive and immersive, weaving together layers of sound to evoke a range of emotions. Since their formation, The Mail has been a fixture in Boston’s music scene, captivating audiences with their electrifying live performances and dynamic stage presence. Their debut album, “Lights On,” released in 2018, received widespread acclaim for its poignant lyricism and infectious melodies. With each release, The Mail continues to push the boundaries of alternative music, exploring new sonic territories while staying true to their roots. As they embark on their musical journey, The Mail invites listeners to join them on a voyage of self-discovery and sonic exploration. The Mail Band Wood & Bone is an Americana roots band based in Massachusetts, led by singer-songwriter Jesse Joseph. The band features a rotating cast of collaborators, with core members Joe Wilkins (guitar, mandolin, vocals), Dennis Monagle (drums, vocals), and Dylan Sullivan (bass, vocals).
