title: Blues Dance Lesson and Social - Blues Union
description: Blues Union is a friendly weekly social partner dance in Union Square, held on Thursdays at 16 Bow St, Somerville, MA 02143 in Dance Union Studio. Partners not required. Come solo, with dance partners, or friends! Blues is a dance form that allows for a great diversity of expression, with a broad vocabulary. It developed along with swing dance in African-American communities as a blend of African and European dance styles. The dance has a heavy focus on partner connection, and connection to the ground with weight and momentum. There is a definite "pulse" as the dancer sinks in with each beat. It is a tonic for the soul. Through it, we can connect to the past, the present, and each other. Each evening includes a 1 hour beginner-friendly lesson before the social dance. (7:00p - 8:00p) Lesson (8:00p - 9:00p) Community Socializing Hour (9:00p - 11:00p) Social Dance Admission is sliding scale, $10-$25 cash or Venmo at door. Presale tickets here: https://withfriends.co/blues_union No one turned away due to lack of funds. For more information, and a week-to-week details, check out our website and Facebook pages. https://www.facebook.com/groups/bluesunion https://bluesunionboston.com/ See you on the dance floor. **Mission** Blues Union’s mission is to cultivate a community around blues dancing, music, and culture in our local community. We aim to foster a culture of curiosity and learning, a culture of understanding and appreciation of blues dance, music, culture, and people–both where it came from and where it is today. Because blues dance is a Black dance, we also commit to center Black voices, to partner with Black musicians, scholars, businesses, and community members, and to use art as an in-road to social change. **Covid-19 & Accessibility** -N95/KN95 or better & vaccination required (masks provided if you don't have one), so as many of our community members as possible can join us on the dance floor. -Code of conduct & covid policies: https://bluesunionboston.com/cod

title: Who Owns AI Governance?
description: Who owns AI Governance? Legal sees a privacy question. Engineering sees a technical one. Risk wants it in the controls framework. On Friday 20 November we launch the AIGI Forum in Boston with a panel built around that question: → Jaimin Patel, OneTrust: governing AI agents, from autonomy and sensitive-data access to permissions and accountability → Benjamin Siegel, Privacy Ref: how privacy laws shape automated decision-making → Sergio Pérez Fernández, Keepler Data Tech: AI governance, end to end Also on the table: internally built AI versus vendor AI versus agents, keeping humans in the loop without burying the governance team, and what the next five years bring. Who is this for? → AI governance leaders and data governance professionals → Business stakeholders responsible for AI adoption → In-house counsel and privacy professionals being asked to sign off on AI → Engineers and AI teams building and deploying agentic systems → Security, risk and compliance leads who own the controls → Anyone starting, or inheriting, an AI governance program The discussion will be followed by a Q&A session. Bring the question your organization hasn't answered yet. Microsoft New England Research & Development Center One Memorial Drive, Cambridge, MA Fri, 20 November · 8:30–11:45 AM EST Networking, panel, Q&A, then more networking. Free to attend. Registration required: https://aigovernanceinternational.org/aigiforum #AIGovernance #AgenticAI #Privacy #ResponsibleAI #AIRisk #AIRegulation #Boston #CambridgeMA

title: Rubies
description: Rubies is a new, intimate collection of stunning minerals, gemstones, and jewelry on display in the Earth & Planetary Sciences Gallery. Ruby, the red variety of the mineral corundum, owes its vibrant color to trace amounts of chromium in its crystal structure. This element also gives many rubies a striking fluorescence, glowing bright crimson under ultraviolet light. Ruby’s internal world—its inclusions, growth zoning, and rutile “silk” needles—records its geological journey and can reveal its origin, making ruby a gemstone of extraordinary beauty and a rich source of scientific insight. title: Collecting Wonders: Tomorrow’s Discoveries
description: When you imagine a museum, you might picture cases of artifacts. But the objects on display at the Harvard Museum of Natural History are a tiny percentage of the total collections. Behind the scenes, experts care for 26 million specimens. These objects form the basis for studying life on Earth. They are records of the planet from different times and places. Objects span billions of years and come from every continent, ocean, and beyond. They are stone and bone, plant and animal, feather and fossil. Since the early days of Harvard University, collections have been central to teaching and research. People continue to study these collections and uncover knowledge. Come explore some treasures of the collection! Explore historic specimens presented to mark the 250th Anniversary of the United States Declaration of Independence on June 27. Would Harvard students in 1776 have known about the things we see and do today? Take a guess, then search for specific objects across our four museums—the Harvard Museum of Natural History, the Peabody Museum of Archaeology & Ethnology, the Harvard Museum of the Ancient Near East, and the Collection of Historical Scientific Instruments—to check your answers. title: SCSB Lunch Series with Dr. Earl Miller: Cognition is analog because the brain is
description: Date: Friday, November 20, 2026 Time: 12:00pm – 1:00pm Location: Simons Center Conference room 46-6011. Zoom: https://mit.zoom.us/j/94709560643 Speaker: Earl K. Miller, Ph.D. Affiliation: Picower Professor of Neuroscience, Picower Institute for Learning and Memory, MIT Talk title: Cognition is analog because the brain is Abstract: Classic models likened brain function to networks of neurons, analogous to telegraph systems. Emerging evidence, however, suggests that higher cognition relies not only on synaptic connections but also on rhythmic oscillations. These “brain waves” are electric field dynamics that travel across the cortex and shape neuronal spiking. This view expands the brain’s functional repertoire: the “telegraph wires” of synaptic circuits also generate “radio waves” (electric fields) that rapidly distribute influence across large distances. Such fields may support large-scale coordination underlying executive control and consciousness. They may even enable energy-efficient analog computation, which may explain why our brains run on the power of a dim lightbulb (20W).

description: *Note: Unusual time and location Speaker: Jennifer Morse (University of Virginia) Title: Macdonald polynomials have nine lives (Current Developments in Mathematics) Abstract: Macdonald polynomials arose in the late 1980s from orthogonal polynomials and constant term identities, and have since led many lives: in generating functions for tableaux, Dyck paths and parking functions; in the representation theory of symmetric groups and the geometry of Hilbert schemes; and in affine Schubert calculus and double affine Hecke algebras, among other places. These lectures trace how Macdonald’s construction and his surprising conjecture that certain coefficients should be counting something inspired several largely separate directions. We will finish with how recent proofs of long-standing conjectures led to a discovery that brings these threads back together and has the potential to set off a new burst of activity.

title: Materials Lab Workshop: Casting Connections—Molds, Replicas, and Questions of Authorship
description: Join research curator Francesca Bewer for a workshop focused on art and science. We’ll explore the intimate connections between models, molds, and casts; how molds and casts have been used to produce, replicate, and preserve three-dimensional objects; and what these objects can teach us about skill, technology, and value. Working with clay, plaster, wax, alginate, and silicone putty, we’ll experiment with different processes of molding and casting. Along the way, you’ll be introduced to the scientific tools used to investigate and identify the traces of process and change. Through discussion and comparison with historical plaster casts, wax models, and other surrogates in the Harvard Art Museums collections, we’ll ask when a copy might be considered “fake,” “genuine,” or something in between, and how replicas support research, teaching, and conservation in museums today. This workshop is one of four offered this fall that explore different media through the lens of art and science. Take one or take them all! The four workshops are: Saturday, September 19: Landscape Drawing with Optical DevicesWednesday, October 7: Color Alchemy—Pigments and DIY PaintFriday, November 6: Making an ImpressionFriday, November 20: Casting Connections—Molds, Replicas, and Questions of Authorship

title: Wang Lecture: Biophysics and Modeling Approaches for Development of Effective Downstream Bioprocesses of Complex Biological Products
description: Speaker: Steven M. Cramer, Institute Professor, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute Steve Cramer is an Institute Professor at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute. His laboratory develops models, materials, and processes to make downstream bioprocessing more effective for the purification of biological products. He is a member of the National Academy of Engineering, UT Austin’s Academy of Distinguished Chemical Engineers and an elected fellow of AAAS, AIChE, ACS and AIMBE. He has won numerous awards, including the Gordon Prize from the NAE, the ACS Separations Science and Technology Award, the BIOT Division’s Michael’s Award, the Gaden Award from Biotechnology and Bioengineering, the Wiley Distinguished Faculty Award and the School of Engineering Outstanding Professor and Research Excellence Awards from RPI. His inventions and models have been employed by numerous companies and he is active on industrial scientific advisory boards. The 65 PhD graduates from the Cramer lab have had a significant impact, with many former students now playing key leadership roles in the state of the art of industrial bioprocessing at major biopharmaceutical and bioseparations companies worldwide as well as in academia.

description: Trauma affects people of all ages, influencing emotional well-being, relationships, and how we navigate life's challenges. Join five distinguished experts from Harvard Medical School, Harvard University, Cambridge Health Alliance, and The Chicago School for an engaging discussion exploring childhood and adult trauma, domestic violence, attachment, mindfulness, Internal Family Systems (IFS), and evidence-informed approaches to healing and resilience. Through clinical insights and research perspectives, attendees will gain a deeper understanding of trauma and discover approaches that support emotional well-being and recovery. A live Q&A will provide an opportunity to engage directly with the speakers. As the holiday season approaches, many individuals and families may be navigating grief, trauma, loneliness, or emotional challenges. This event aims to make mental health education accessible to those who may benefit most. Completely FREE and open to everyone worldwide, regardless of Harvard affiliation.

After growing up steeped in the Boston Celtic music scene, these five young women began touring at an early age, quickly enchanting domestic and international audiences with their youthful enthusiasm, creative arrangements, and sensitive performances. From the sweetness of newfound love to jealousy, heartbreak, and unexpected joy, the evening traces the course of true love through some of the Baroque’s most expressive and exhilarating music. title: Rubies
description: Rubies is a new, intimate collection of stunning minerals, gemstones, and jewelry on display in the Earth & Planetary Sciences Gallery. Ruby, the red variety of the mineral corundum, owes its vibrant color to trace amounts of chromium in its crystal structure. This element also gives many rubies a striking fluorescence, glowing bright crimson under ultraviolet light. Ruby’s internal world—its inclusions, growth zoning, and rutile “silk” needles—records its geological journey and can reveal its origin, making ruby a gemstone of extraordinary beauty and a rich source of scientific insight. Check the museum's website for closure dates.

title: Collecting Wonders: Tomorrow’s Discoveries
description: When you imagine a museum, you might picture cases of artifacts. But the objects on display at the Harvard Museum of Natural History are a tiny percentage of the total collections. Behind the scenes, experts care for 26 million specimens. These objects form the basis for studying life on Earth. They are records of the planet from different times and places. Objects span billions of years and come from every continent, ocean, and beyond. They are stone and bone, plant and animal, feather and fossil. Since the early days of Harvard University, collections have been central to teaching and research. People continue to study these collections and uncover knowledge. Come explore some treasures of the collection! Explore historic specimens presented to mark the 250th Anniversary of the United States Declaration of Independence on June 27. Check museum's website for closure dates.

title: Beginner to Intermediate Modern Connections
description: Modern Connections is a Horton based modern dance technique class taught at a pace designed for the students in the room. Class begins with sequential and consistent warm-up, continues with center phrases that are designed to promote competence and growth of proper technique. Students build the necessary vocabulary and body awareness required for Flat Back, Lateral T, and Fortifications through proper corrections focused on alignment and detailed explanations of the initiation of movements. Cost: $20 Single Class (Saturday) | $72 for 4 Class Discount *NEW* The Dance Complex requires ALL visitors to have a Membership, Guest Pass, or $5 Day Pass to access the building. REGISTER HERE Accepted Payments: Vagaro (through registration link listed above) What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? Unfortunately 2-3 sentences is inadequate to articulate the legacy of the style that I teach inclusive of history, cultural and geographic origin, but I do think that if folks are looking for more information about the Horton technique that I base my teachings around, they can use these resources to start: http://www.dancehistoryproject.org/index-of-artists/lester-horton/ & https://www.britannica.com/biography/Lester-Horton What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? I began my formal training in Modern Dance 25yrs ago during my undergrad at Dean College under the tutelage of Nailah Randall-Bellinger. There I studied Limon, Graham, Dunham, Cunningham and Horton techniques. I continued my training in various programs and have worked with a variety of choreographers and genres post grad. Those experiences influence my comprehension of body mechanics and approach towards conveying information. I decided to attend the Horton Pedagogy program at the Alvin Ailey School and from there have taken a deep dive into my pedagogical approach that is able to reach students no matter where they are in their training. title: Waack ‘n’ Bootz: Rhythm and Runway Series
description: This class is for people who wish to become better performers, runway artists and posing artists. This class is also for dancers who want to learn the techniques of Waacking. Both classes require similar foundation. Runway is when a model struts down the aisle in designer clothing or a fashion created look. Their job is to sell the garment, and to exude absolute style on the runway. This class will help students through whatever they are going through in life with a walk. I believe that when we walk or move ahead, we conquer our fears just by moving forward. This class will help you learn how to flow with rhythm, pose with intention and twirl in grace. Waacking is a style that can be used on any runway, stage or platform. It’s rooted in Queer gay club culture and was fine tuned through underground disco music by gay men who had dance through exclusion and slurs. Waacking derived from Punking and has evolved into today’s dance culture all over the world. In this dance we will learn how to develop musicality, rhythmic arm patterns, and how to ooze out our emotions while creating visual art. This class will help students dance on cue, freestyle, and learn the rhythm of Waacking. But most of all, you will learn work the floor with this dance. African and Caribbean dance traditions are rooted in the diverse cultures of countries such as Madagascar, Senegal, Ghana, Nigeria, Côte d’Ivoire, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Haiti, Jamaica, Trinidad & Tobago, and Cuba, among many others. Tap dancing began as an answer to the horrors of colonial enslavement…with no musical instruments, Irish and West African slaves turned to their own feet to create rhythms and percussion while pulling movement and technique from traditional tribal and cultural dances. Sounds were initially made with wooden soles, then pennies and bottle caps, finally becoming the modern metal plates screwed to the ball and heel of the shoes. These dances made their way to minstrel and vaudeville shows, eventually transforming into the broadway and rhythm style tap dancing we know today. Flamenco is a form of song, dance, and instrumental (mostly guitar) music commonly associated with the Andalusian Roma (Gypsies) of southern Spain. (There, the Roma people are called Gitanos.) The roots of flamenco, though somewhat mysterious, seem to lie in the Roma migration from Rajasthan (in northwest India) to Spain between the 9th and 14th centuries. These migrants brought with them musical instruments, such as tambourines, bells, and wooden castanets, and an extensive repertoire of songs and dances. In Spain they encountered the rich cultures of the Sephardic Jews and the Moors. Their centuries-long cultural intermingling produced the unique art form known as flamenco. (https://www.britannica.com/art/flamenco) What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? I have been dancing and performing flamenco professionally for over 30 years. I have studied both here and in Spain, and continue my studies (to keep current with the dance) at various workshops both here and abroad. I was the first to teach Capoeira in New England. Mestre Joao Pequenho certified me as a teacher of Capoeira Angola in 1991. Contra Mestre Calango: I moved to Boston in 2000 to continue training with Mestre Deraldo. Since then, I traveled with him to universities and events around the world to assist in demonstrating and teaching of the beautiful art of Capoeira Angola. I graduated as a Contra Mestre in 2017. title: Ashes and Diamonds
description: Directed by Andrzej Wajda, 1958. The last and loudest entry in Wajda’s WWII trilogy, Ashes and Diamonds adapts Jerzy Andrzejewski’s eponymous 1948 novel into one of Polish cinema’s strongest and most celebrated works. Set on May 8, 1945—Victory Day in Europe—after Red Army battalions had already expelled the occupier out of Poland, the historical thriller stars anti-Communist Home Army insurgents in a doomed underground plot to resist Soviet rule. In his performance as militant Maciek, Zbigniew Cybulski approaches and at times surpasses the youthful, tragic cool of James Dean, while Jerzy Wójcik’s stark camerawork ignites an inflammatory script into Wajda’s fiercest unraveling of national myth and taboo. Overflowing with Christian symbolism, the film was the director’s proudest achievement; it remains to this day a widely discussed touchstone of the Polish Film School and one of modern cinema’s richest interrogations of agency and belief in the face of futility and (overwhelming, ambivalent) defeat. Part of the series Once There Was History . Andrzej Wajda at 100.

title: STUDIO STAGE: Ana Ospina-Edwards, cello | Echoes | Graduating Student Project
description: Ana is a Boston-based cellist and educator from Colombia. She combines performance, teaching, and arts administration, serving as cello faculty at Attacca School of Music and The New School of Muisc, and coordinating Longy’s Side-by-Side program. Passionate about multicultural chamber music, she promotes concerts featuring underrepresented composers and performs solo works that highlight the cello’s versatility across diverse traditions. She plays with Boston-area orchestras, including the Boston Chamber Symphony and Du Bois Orchestra, where she is Personnel Manager. She is also the cellist of the Eric Hofbauer Quintet (EHX), whose 2026 album blends rock, jazz, and new wave with social and cultural themes centered on reconnection through music. An Equity Scholar at Longy pursuing a graduate diploma, Ana is committed to using music to foster multicultural dialogue and strengthen community connections through her multifaceted artistic journey. Ana Ospina-Edwards is a student of Christine Lamprea and Jean-Michel Fonteneau. Studio Stage Series Studio Stage is your chance to experience the thrill of discovery. Here, emerging artists take the stage to share their ideas, test their creativity, and invite you into their artistic journey. Each performance features Longy students presenting works in progress, a core part of their training and an expression of Longy’s academic and performance mission. These performances are alive with the energy and excitement of music in the making, and you get to be there as the next generation of musicians finds its voice. Longy’s performances are free and open to the public, but please register in advance.

title: Comedy Harbor Presents: Mike Cannon - The Early Show
description: Come see the hilarious Mike Cannon! One of the best comedians working today. In Boston for one night only, see you at the early or late show! Mike Cannon is a New York City–based comedian, podcaster, writer, and actor. He has headlined some of the world’s most iconic venues, including a sold-out hometown performance at Gramercy Theatre, the footage of which he released in full on YouTube in 2025. Mike currently co-hosts the parenting and career podcast Beautiful Boys with fellow comedian Andy Haynes, as well as the preposterously titled Fart Carnival with best friend and frequent collaborator Brendan Sagalow. In 2023, he served as a contributing producer, writer, and panelist on Vice TV’s Super Maximum Retro Show , hosted by Chris Distefano. His latest stand-up special, Traumatized Animal (2024), has amassed hundreds of thousands of views on YouTube, millions of views across social media, and widespread acclaim from fans and critics alike. Mike also hosts several original digital series on his YouTube channel, including Coach Cannon , Comedians Taking Edibles and Doing Crowd Work , and his road documentary series, Spots . In 2022, Mike released two independently-produced hour specials on YouTube: Mike Cannon’s Huge Mistake , a crowd work special fueled by edibles, and White Privilege Homeless . Both earned praise from audiences, fellow comedians, and critics. His debut special, Life Begins , premiered on YouTube in 2020 and was named one of Laugh Button’s Top 35 Comedy Specials of the year. The accompanying album, released by 800 Pound Gorilla Records, was recognized as one of Interrobang’s Top 11 Comedy Albums of 2020 and one of SiriusXM Raw Dog Radio’s Top 10 Comedy Albums of the year. Mike’s first comedy album, I Think It Just Kicked In , debuted at #1 on the iTunes Comedy chart, #7 on the Billboard Comedy chart and has been streamed more than five million times. Outside of stand-up, Mike received critical acclaim for his lead performance in the feature film Timi

title: Laurie MacAllister & Seth Glier
description: In late 2024, Laurie MacAllister embarked on an exciting new chapter, launching a solo career with a sold-out performance right here at legendary Club Passim. Two decades earlier, she co-founded the beloved Americana trio Red Molly, which released seven acclaimed albums and toured both the U.S. and internationally, including appearances at MerleFest, Cayamo, and Boston Symphony Hall. Along the way, ad executives heard Laurie’s voice on the Red Molly album “Never Been to Vegas” and invited her to sing the iconic Folgers Coffee jingle for a national TV commercial. Her 2018 self-produced solo album “The Lies the Poets Tell” is a heartfelt tribute to the contemporary folk music scene, celebrating a handful of its best songs and songwriters. It features duets with six male artists, including the late Americana master Jimmy LaFave. SiriusXM praised the album as “Defining. A curated collection packed with emotional vibrancy.” Laurie’s earlier solo album “The Things I Choose To Do” was produced by folk luminary Cliff Eberhardt and was first released independently. Hearing it, Barnes & Noble re-released it as an exclusive on their label, saying, “MacAllister wholly inhabits these songs as subtly as a chameleon, convincingly taking on the persona’s skin, quite simply singing her heart out.” From a young girl with a quiet dream of becoming a singer, Laurie’s journey has unfolded one song at a time. Over more than two decades, she’s made her dream into a reality.

title: A Generation
description: Directed by Andrzej Wajda, 1955. After witnessing Nazis slay his friend, young proletarian Stach joins a partisan resistance cell (the left-wing People’s Guard) and transforms as a person, lover and antifascist. Andrzej Wajda’s feature debut exudes energy and composure, shading 1942 Warsaw in Expressionist cinematography—courtesy of Jerzy Lipman—and a contrapuntal soundscape by the modernist composer Andrzej Markowski. Influences of Italian neorealism and urban documentary are apparent, as is Wajda’s ambition to devise a new Polish cinema on the ruins of the old and artificial. No actors with experience in prewar filmmaking were used; A Generation was the first professional project for most of the cast and crew. To appropriately imbue spaces with atmospheric dread, filming mostly took place on cloudy and rainy days, ensuring that Wajda’s first film is also among his darkest. Assistant director Kazimierz Kutz, meanwhile, provided one of film history’s earliest appearances of the “squib”—here, a condom filled with fake blood and dynamite, a technique used with explosive success to this day. Part of the series Once There Was History . Andrzej Wajda at 100.

title: Collecting Wonders: Tomorrow’s Discoveries
description: When you imagine a museum, you might picture cases of artifacts. But the objects on display at the Harvard Museum of Natural History are a tiny percentage of the total collections. Behind the scenes, experts care for 26 million specimens. These objects form the basis for studying life on Earth. They are records of the planet from different times and places. Objects span billions of years and come from every continent, ocean, and beyond. They are stone and bone, plant and animal, feather and fossil. Since the early days of Harvard University, collections have been central to teaching and research. People continue to study these collections and uncover knowledge. Come explore some treasures of the collection! Explore historic specimens presented to mark the 250th Anniversary of the United States Declaration of Independence on June 27. Check museum's website for closure dates.

title: Rubies
description: Rubies is a new, intimate collection of stunning minerals, gemstones, and jewelry on display in the Earth & Planetary Sciences Gallery. Ruby, the red variety of the mineral corundum, owes its vibrant color to trace amounts of chromium in its crystal structure. This element also gives many rubies a striking fluorescence, glowing bright crimson under ultraviolet light. Ruby’s internal world—its inclusions, growth zoning, and rutile “silk” needles—records its geological journey and can reveal its origin, making ruby a gemstone of extraordinary beauty and a rich source of scientific insight. Check the museum's website for closure dates.

title: Pop Quiz: 1776
description: Step back into the 18th century and put your detective skills to the test! Pop Quiz: 1776 takes you on a four-museum adventure to uncover surprising ways that life at Harvard was both similar to and—or different from —today. Would Harvard students in 1776 have known about the things we see and do today? Take a guess, then search for specific objects across our four museums—the Harvard Museum of Natural History, the Peabody Museum of Archaeology & Ethnology, the Harvard Museum of the Ancient Near East, and the Collection of Historical Scientific Instruments—to check your answers. Pro tip: join us any Sunday–Friday 11:00 am–4:00 pm to access all four museums! Check museum's website for closure dates.

title: Innocent Sorcerers
description: Directed by Andrzej Wajda, 1960. Wajda’s singular New Wave film—shot two months before À bout de souffle but released after—follows a noncommittal hipster through a series of pararomantic encounters in nightclubs, apartments and boxing rings. Dismissed both by early critics and the director (who subsequently called the early ’60s the “most difficult period” of his life), Innocent Sorcerers has since been reappraised as a key entry in postwar Polish cinema. Youth culture, jazz, motorbikes and promiscuity abound in a freshly-thawed Warsaw under the influence of Western capital and culture. History and politics are absent, with Wajda’s attention turned instead to the contemporary music scene he and then-twenty-year-old screenwriter Jerzy Skolimowski experienced at the Łódź Film School. Pianist Krzysztof Komeda composed the electrifying score and played himself in a cameo, where Zbigniew Cybulski also makes an appearance. One of Wajda’s liveliest films is also one of his best, soured only by a happy ending didactically tacked on at the eleventh hour by censors. Part of the series Once There Was History . Andrzej Wajda at 100.

title: Harvard Square French Fry & Pairings Food Tour
description: Harvard Square is famous for so much — Harvard University, eclectic bookshops, buskers, and a food scene that punches well above its weight. But here’s what most visitors don’t know: it’s also home to some of the best french fries in all of Massachusetts . Together with our guide Larom, a Harvard alum, we built an entire tour around that fact, and it’s become one of the most unique food experiences in Cambridge. On this 90-minute walking adventure, you’ll sample distinctly different styles of fries at three beloved Harvard Square spots — from classic hand-cut wedges to smoky BBQ fries to legendary sweet potato fries — each paired with a drink chosen specifically to bring out the flavors. We’ll try the original raspberry lime rickey , a refreshing peach lemonade , and a crazy ice cream frappe that has to be seen to be believed. All pairings are non-alcoholic, making this tour genuinely fun for the whole family. Along the way, your guide will walk you through the beloved cobblestone streets past Harvard Yard , the Widener Library , the quirky Harvard Lampoon building , and the storied Harvard Faculty Club — sharing the funny, fresh, and occasionally absurd stories that make this neighborhood unlike anywhere else in Boston. You’ll also hear the full saga of the French Fry Wars of the late 20th Century , a deliciously bizarre chapter of local food history that explains why Harvard Square’s fry scene is what it is today. This food tour is ideal for: Visitors to Boston looking for a memorable, off-the-beaten-path Cambridge experience Families with kids and teens who want something interactive and delicious Date nights — quirky, fun, and plenty of good food Birthday celebrations and small group outings Local students, grad students, alums, and neighbors who want to see a new side of Harvard!

description: Somerville Media Center recently received an FY27 Creative Experiences grant from the Massachusetts Cultural Council , and this class series is part of how that funding comes to life. The grant helps us keep Women in Film free and accessible for women in Somerville and the greater Boston area by supporting instruction, an accessible venue, and accessibility services. In this workshop , we’ll look at why women’s voices have been missing from cinema, from the Male Gaze theory to systemic industry barriers, and start building the camera and production skills to tell your own stories. It’s open to women and gender non-conforming people at all skill levels. No experience needed, just your creativity and a willingness to learn. Important: This class is a prerequisite for the Women in Film filmmaking group , our 12-week hands-on cohort covering camera, sound, editing, and storytelling, which ends with a public community screening. description: Julia Minkin SHOW DESCRIPTION: Chicago-based singer-songwriter Julia Minkin is joined by Boston favorites Bowling Shoes and Cate Yoder for an evening of inventive indie music, compelling storytelling, and rich, genre-bending sounds. From shimmering synth-pop and art-rock experimentation to intimate folk melodies, this lineup offers music that’s as intelligent as it is fun. ARTIST BIOS: Julia Minken: Best known for co-writing viral hit songs with French electropop sensation Kid Francescoli, Chicago-based singer-songwriter Julia Minkin steps into her own with her debut album Not Ready, co-created and produced with her husband Andrew Sudhibhasilp. Blending warm, folk-tinged vocals with nostalgic dance-floor energy and introspection, Minkin “finds her own creative voice, shimmering, rhythmic, and heartfelt—both bold and refreshingly sincere” (Thoughts Words Actions). Bowling Shoes: Melding innovative art-pop experimentalism with indie-rock nuance and arena-ready hooks, Boston, MA’s Bowling Shoes craft eminently catchy music sprinkled with delightful touches of subversive noise Cate Yoder: A double and electric bassist and guitarist from Richmond, Virginia, Cate Yoder learns about her environment through exploring, inventing, and performing a multitude of genres or really any music she can get hands on. Since being established primarily as a bass player, she is diving into the songwriting indie folk role with her band of talented women, performing in the Boston area. With airy melodies, detailed guitar, piano, and percussive elements, and bitter lyrics, she hopes to share her experience of finding solace and comfort in a complex world. description: The Lizard Lounge Poetry Jam with feature Jimmy Tingle Nov 22nd! $10 Jimmy Tingle is a comedian, producer, and commentator who has provided commentaries for 60 Minutes II, MSNBC, and Boston stations WBUR, GBH and WBZ. As a comedian, he has appeared on The Tonight Show, Conan O’Brien, PBS, NPR’s Fresh Air with Terry Gross, Comedy Central, Veep, The Moth and in his own HBO half-hour comedy special. He is a graduate of UMass Dartmouth (77) and Harvard’s Kennedy School of Government, where he was the Harvard Graduate School commencement speaker for the class in 2010. He is the founder of Humor for Humanity, a social enterprise that raises spirits, funds, and awareness for nonprofits and social causes through his work as an emcee, comedian, producer, and auctioneer. He is a former candidate for Lieutenant Governor of Massachusetts, and he received 41% of the vote in the Massachusetts Democratic primary as a first-time candidate for public office. His latest film is a self-produced comedy documentary JIMMY TINGLE: The “Radical” Middle- Why Would a Comedian Run for Office? The film is based on his campaign for Lieutenant Governor of Massachusetts. Additional documentary film work includes the International Emmy Award Winning Damned in the USA, Channel 4, UK; America with the Top Down, Channel 4, UK, PBS; When Stand up Stood Out, THINKFilm; Call Me Lucky, Amazon Prime; and Jimmy Tingle’s American Dream, written and produced by Jimmy and directed by Vincent Straggas of Flag Day Productions. Feature film work includes Head of State starring Chris Rock; Clear History starring Larry David; Boondock Saints starring Willem Dafoe and Next Stop Wonderland with Hope Davis. title: Luis Reyes Quintet / The Quantum Collective
description: $15 admission / $10 for students / 10pm doors / 10:30 show / seated Luis Reyes Quintet Led by saxophonist and composer Luis Reyes, the quintet is an ensemble of musicians from Boston's vibrant jazz community. Performing original compositions that draw from a wide range of influences, from hard bop to modern jazz, the group embraces the depth of the jazz tradition while exploring the possibilities of contemporary improvisation. With a sound that is both rooted in tradition and forward-looking, the quintet reflects the diverse and evolving spirit of modern jazz. @luisreyes_saxophone The Quantum Collective A brainchild of local trumpeter Matt Kelly, The Quantum Collective bursts with energy and vitality, trying to capture the urgency of this moment through the lens of Black American Music. The quintet eschews the electronic experimentation of sister band Quantum Moon for a more grounded and tactile approach. Taking cues from visionary musicians and activists like Max Roach, Gil Scott-Heron, and Sons of Kemet, The Quantum Collective leans into the fact that making music is an inherently political act and every note can be a barb in the side of an authoritarian institution while also capturing the joy and resilience in our hearts. So come dig deep and let loose in joyful rage and beautiful sadness. @mattkellytrumpet mattkellytrumpet.com

It reflects our belief that healing is a right — not a privilege — and that healing happens most sustainably when care is consistent, culturally grounded, and rooted in community. title: Sylvia Lavin, "Architecture After Fire"
description: This lecture, “Architecture After Fire,” argues that the rise of American architectural modernism was inseparable from the forest, not because of the use of timber, but because of modernism’s reliance on arboreal media—employing trees as information and communication systems and as metaphors. Tracking the white pine through deforestation, wildfire, and the formation of the Chicago school, this paper explores the series of substitutions, each triggered by fire, that converted environmental catastrophe into aesthetic doctrine and designated these operations as the primary function of modern architecture, artistically considered.

description: Classes teach Broadway style tap and focus on repetitive technique to encourage muscle memory and the confidence to create clear sounds. Inclusion is a priority so that all students feel welcome. Classes are “drop-in”, meaning you may join any week and there’s no “semester” commitment. Past steps are always reviewed with the introduction of 1 or 2 new steps or combos each class. Accepted Payments: Cash, Venmo (@christina-harrington-7) What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? Tap dancing began as an answer to the horrors of colonial enslavement…with no musical instruments, Irish and West African slaves turned to their own feet to create rhythms and percussion while pulling movement and technique from traditional tribal and cultural dances. Sounds were initially made with wooden soles, then pennies and bottle caps, finally becoming the modern metal plates screwed to the ball and heel of the shoes. These dances made their way to minstrel and vaudeville shows, eventually transforming into the broadway and rhythm style tap dancing we know today. title: Kanał
description: Directed by Andrzej Wajda, 1957. Gripping and tenebrous, Andrzej Wajda’s second feature resumes A Generation ’s interest in naturalist, anti-dogmatic tellings of wartime resistance, yet shifts focus to the underground Home Army, whose 1944 Warsaw Uprising was a pivotal (if ultimately doomed) attempt at liberation. The first film to tackle the tragic and contentious operation, Kanał descends into the capital’s sewers to observe the hopeless, Dantesque trek of exhausted platoons escaping the city in late September, when defeat was already inescapable. Jerzy Lipman returns as cinematographer, depicting the dank gutters—all built in the back lot of a Łódź studio—in an asphyxiating high-contrast palette. To make the film, Wajda benefitted from Gomułka’s Thaw which, however, did little to shield Kanał from harsh audience critique. “This film could not satisfy them,” Wajda later remarked. “They had licked their wounds, mourned their dead, and now they wanted to see their moral and spiritual victory, and not death in the sewers.” Unredemptive to its core, Wajda’s bleakest has since been rightfully recognized as one of world cinema’s great reckonings with impossible (yet necessary) roads to freedom. Part of the series Once There Was History . Andrzej Wajda at 100. Screening on film.

title: Boulez at 100
description: As part of the worldwide celebration of Pierre Boulez’s centenary, acclaimed pianists Gloria Cheng and Ralph van Raat bring their touring program Boulez at 100 to MIT, hosted by MIT Media Lab Faculty Director Tod Machover. The program interweaves Boulez’s seminal piano works with music by John Cage, Morton Feldman, Frank Zappa, Magnus Lindberg, and Olivier Messiaen–composers who each echo, anticipate, or challenge Boulez’s vision across modernist, experimental, and boundary-crossing traditions. Featuring chapters from Boulez’s rarely heard Structures Books I and II, the concert traces the rich artistic dialogue between Boulez and the composers whose music surrounds his own. Together, these works reveal Boulez not only as one of the twentieth century’s most influential composers, but also as an artist whose ideas have an increasing, surprising potential to resonate across generations, genres, and musical traditions.

description: $15 @ the door / $10 students / 8:30 start / 8pm doors / seated Jerry Bergonzi , Tenor Saxophone Luther Gray , Drums Plamen Karadonev, Piano Sean Farias, Bass Special Guest , Trumpet A fine, high-powered tenor saxophonist with a tone influenced by John Coltrane, a mastery of chord changes, and a strong musical imagination, Jerry Bergonzi has long had an underground following in the Boston area. He started on clarinet when he was eight, switching to alto at 12, and finally to tenor two years later. Bergonzi was inspired early on by Sonny Rollins, Coltrane, and Hank Mobley. He attended Lowell University and then after graduation played electric bass in local bands behind singers and strippers, saving up enough money to move to New York in 1972. After struggling in the Big Apple for seven years and gaining some recognition as a member of Two Generations of Brubeck and of the Dave Brubeck Quartet (with whom he appeared on several Concord albums during 1979-1981), Bergonzi moved back to Boston in 1981, where he developed a strong career both as a tenorman and as an educator. He has since led several groups (including two called Con Brio and Gonz) and recorded for the Plug, Not Fat, Red, and Blue Note labels. — By Scott Yanow, AllMusic Continuing Every Monday at 8:30pm Lineup subject to change

title: Voices Unheard
description: Voices Unheard SHOW DESCRIPTION: Voices Unheard: From the Margins to the Mic returns to Massachusetts for its seventh consecutive year, continuing its tradition of centering lived experience through story. The event features true narratives from adult storytellers who have submitted their work, sharing personal accounts of identity, origin, separation, and reunion. While participants come from a range of lived experiences—including adoption, foster care, donor conception, and unexpected family discoveries—the lineup reflects those who have chosen to step forward and share their stories this year. Together, these voices create a collective portrait of what it means to grow up without full access to one’s origins, and the ongoing search for connection, meaning, and belonging. ARTIST BIO: Lisa “LC” Coppola is a domestic DCF adoptee, writer, educator, and creator of the Voices Unheard Storytelling Program. She is the author of Voices Unheard: A Reflective Journal for Adult Adoptees and the essay Heartichoke, featured in the 2026 anthology Relative Strangers: Inheritance, Identity, and the Meaning of Kinship. Her debut novel, Monster Flower, is forthcoming from Jaded Ibis Press in Spring 2027. Kristal Parke is a talented filmmaker, producer, speaker and podcaster whose work explores identity, belonging, and resilience. A transracial adoptee from a closed adoption, her personal journey fuels her storytelling with authenticity, compassion, and truth. She creates space for unheard voices, shaping narratives that educate, challenge, inspire and heal. description: Father Of Peace is here. Formed by childhood best friends Avshalom Ariel [Vocals & Guitar] and Tom Bollig [Vocals & Drums] in 2023, and joined by newest member May Alpert [Vocals & Bass] in 2025, the trio move as one, drawn toward something just beyond reach. Their music feels both ancient and immediate – raw, explosive, and melodic, built to be experienced as much as heard. description: Based on the true story of Katherine Ann Power and Clare Schroeder, this gripping new drama follows two women bound by a single, life-altering moment. It’s 1970. College student Power joins an activist group to protest the war. When their resistance turns deadly, Schroeder must grow up in the shadow of her father’s murder while Power disappears and spends decades on the FBI’s Most Wanted List. title: Red McAdam
description: On Comic Western Gothic, Red McAdam’s playful outsider country music shines; he presents an inventive vision of what the genre can be. description: Class begins with a thorough set of exercises at the barre that last from 30 to 45 minutes. Centre practice follows, and may consist of a battement tendu exercise, a battement jeté exercise, a grand battement exercise, small and/or large adage, stationary turns, traveling turns, and petite and grand allegro enchaînement (small and big jumps). Classes are structured so that the dancer warms up their feet, legs, hips and upper body gradually. As class progresses there are more changes of weight and eventually, sudden changes of direction. Live music is provided by a pianist, that ranges from classical pieces to selections from ballet repertoire to improvisational contemporary music. Ballet originated in the Italian Renaissance courts around 1500 as large balls or spectacles that were performed by members of the royal court. The French king, Louis XIV, created the first academy and the positions, steps, and movements of the ballet were collected and codified. The spectacles began to be performed by artists that were trained in the academy, originally as part of an opera, and later as ballets that told a story through music, mime, and dance. Over the centuries ballet has influenced folk dance styles of many (mainly European) nations and, more recently, has been influenced by folk, modern, and contemporary forms of dance from all countries. I had a professional dance career that spanned more than twenty years and included company work in both ballet and contemporary companies as well as dancing, choreographing, and teaching as a freelance artist.

title: Live Blues & Roots Music Returns to Harvard Square: Wednesday Nights @ The Sea Hag Restaurant & Bar
description: The Sea Hag Restaurant & Bar and The Barrett Anderson Band are excited to announce a new weekly series, Blues & Roots Wednesdays , bringing live music back home to historic Harvard Square. “Cambridge, our fair city, and I share deep roots, and I’m thrilled to find a new musical home at The Sea Hag,” says Massachusetts-based singer/guitarist, Barrett Anderson. “Good music and good food are two of our most basic, fundamental needs,” he continues, “What great joy they give us. I am so happy to revel in that every Wednesday night with my dearest musical friends, and Kari and her incredible team at The Sea Hag. We go way back together, and I can’t imagine all the fun we have ahead.” Indeed, Anderson has strong connections to this scene. He remembers: “My first professional experience came when I was 15, backing up Muddy Waters’ band alums Pinetop Perkins and Bob Margolin at the original House of Blues on Winthrop Street. A few months after that I began busking, you’d often find me in Brattle Square or by the pit. This would have been mid/late 90s.” While still a teen, Anderson was a member of The Monster Mike Welch Band and Ronnie Earl & The Broadcasters (“Ronnie was my guitar hero. Then he was my teacher, then my boss. Now he’s my musical Father,” Anderson says), before eventually starting The Barrett Anderson Band in 2007. Anderson won a Boston Music Award (2013 Blues Artist of the Year), was on the Billboard charts (2020’s live album Hynoboogie spent 3 weeks on the Billboard Blues Album chart, peaking at #6), and was nominated for a Blues Music Award (2023 Band of the Year with Anthony Geraci & The Boston Blues All-Stars), all the while playing nationally, internationally, and locally in Cambridge and the greater Boston area. In addition to the musical roots, long-time locals may recognize Anderson from a decade serving tables and bartending at The Sea Hag’s sister establishment, Grendel’s Den, or from Abodeon, the mid-century modern shop started by his family. title: Harvard Square French Fry & Pairings Food Tour
description: Harvard Square is famous for so much — Harvard University, eclectic bookshops, buskers, and a food scene that punches well above its weight. But here’s what most visitors don’t know: it’s also home to some of the best french fries in all of Massachusetts . Together with our guide Larom, a Harvard alum, we built an entire tour around that fact, and it’s become one of the most unique food experiences in Cambridge. On this 90-minute walking adventure, you’ll sample distinctly different styles of fries at three beloved Harvard Square spots — from classic hand-cut wedges to smoky BBQ fries to legendary sweet potato fries — each paired with a drink chosen specifically to bring out the flavors. We’ll try the original raspberry lime rickey , a refreshing peach lemonade , and a crazy ice cream frappe that has to be seen to be believed. All pairings are non-alcoholic, making this tour genuinely fun for the whole family. Along the way, your guide will walk you through the beloved cobblestone streets past Harvard Yard , the Widener Library , the quirky Harvard Lampoon building , and the storied Harvard Faculty Club — sharing the funny, fresh, and occasionally absurd stories that make this neighborhood unlike anywhere else in Boston. You’ll also hear the full saga of the French Fry Wars of the late 20th Century , a deliciously bizarre chapter of local food history that explains why Harvard Square’s fry scene is what it is today. This food tour is ideal for: Visitors to Boston looking for a memorable, off-the-beaten-path Cambridge experience Families with kids and teens who want something interactive and delicious Date nights — quirky, fun, and plenty of good food Birthday celebrations and small group outings Local students, grad students, alums, and neighbors who want to see a new side of Harvard!

title: The Promised Land
description: Directed by Andrzej Wajda, 1975. “The Pope—now that’s a company!” One of the great films about capitalism, Wajda’s The Promised Land turns Nobel laureate Władysław Reymont’s 1899 novel into a three-hour epic of finance, opportunism and deception. In 1880s Łódź, three entrepreneurial men set out to ride the Industrial Revolution by opening a cotton processing plant, enriching (and irredeemably destroying) themselves in the process. Extreme wide-angle lensing—which Wajda had already employed to great effect in The Ashes —turns looms and mills into ominous objects, further made alien by Wojciech Kilar’s avant-garde score. Locations were effortless to source, as Łódź—Poland’s answer to Manchester—had kept early factory interiors intact, machines and offices included. In adapting Reymont, Wajda aimed to expunge the plot of ethnic stereotypes, traces of which nevertheless remain. So too does the director’s ambition to make what he called an “American” film, edited with zest, suspense and more than a little unabashed spectacle (as well as gore). Part of the series Once There Was History . Andrzej Wajda at 100.

title: Sewing 101 (Main)
description: In this 90-minute workshop, you’ll learn the basics of sewing machine operation and safety. This session will cover machine setup, basic functions, threading the machine, reloading the bobbin, sewing straight stitches, and recognizing when stitch tension has gone awry. As we learn together, we’ll work on a simple sewing project—a drawstring bag—which most students will be able to complete by the end of the class. You must complete Hive Safety Training before registering for this workshop. If you have not completed the training, you will be removed from the class—even if you plan to take it later. The class is designed for all levels, from beginners to experienced dancers, with modifications and repetition that allow everyone to participate at their own pace. Sylver’s teaching philosophy is rooted in creating a welcoming, judgment-free environment where students can connect with the music, move freely, build confidence, and have fun while getting a great workout. title: Beginner and Intermediate Tap for All Levels
description: Classes teach Broadway style tap and focus on repetitive technique to encourage muscle memory and the confidence to create clear sounds. Inclusion is a priority so that all students feel welcome. Classes are “drop-in”, meaning you may join any week and there’s no “semester” commitment. Past steps are always reviewed with the introduction of 1 or 2 new steps or combos each class. Similar to a yoga class, students work at their own individual levels and build up skill at their own pace. Beginners will feel comfortable regardless of when they join. Cost: $20 for 1 hour | $25 for 90 minutes *NEW* The Dance Complex requires ALL visitors to have a Membership, Guest Pass, or $5 Day Pass to access the building. Registration: Email or text Christina Harrington to register: charrington9901@gmail.com | (617) 852-6240 Pre-registration is encouraged but not required. Drop-ins are welcome. Accepted Payments: Cash, Venmo (@christina-harrington-7) What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? Tap dancing began as an answer to the horrors of colonial enslavement…with no musical instruments, Irish and West African slaves turned to their own feet to create rhythms and percussion while pulling movement and technique from traditional tribal and cultural dances. Sounds were initially made with wooden soles, then pennies and bottle caps, finally becoming the modern metal plates screwed to the ball and heel of the shoes. These dances made their way to minstrel and vaudeville shows, eventually transforming into the broadway and rhythm style tap dancing we know today. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? Christina Harrington joined The Dance Complex as a Teaching Artist in May 2012. As a child she studied tap, jazz, and ballet at the Paula Coffey Dance Center in East Bridgewater, MA from 1987-1995 where tap was always her favorite. title: Flamenco Technique/Choreography Class with Sabrina Avilés
description: Classes will begin with a focus on technique, followed by choreography incorporating the mantón de Manila. This class is best suited for students with prior experience working with a mantón and will culminate in a performance in the spring. Cost: $35 Single Class | $224 Entire Series (7 classes) REGISTER HERE What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? Flamenco is a form of song, dance, and instrumental (mostly guitar) music commonly associated with the Andalusian Roma (Gypsies) of southern Spain. (There, the Roma people are called Gitanos.) The roots of flamenco, though somewhat mysterious, seem to lie in the Roma migration from Rajasthan (in northwest India) to Spain between the 9th and 14th centuries. These migrants brought with them musical instruments, such as tambourines, bells, and wooden castanets, and an extensive repertoire of songs and dances. In Spain they encountered the rich cultures of the Sephardic Jews and the Moors. Their centuries-long cultural intermingling produced the unique art form known as flamenco. (https://www.britannica.com/art/flamenco) What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? I have been dancing and performing flamenco professionally for over 30 years. Throughout my career, I was also a member of three local flamenco companies: Ramon de los Reyes Spanish Dance Theatre, Omayra Amaya Flamenco Sin Limites and my own company, Flamenco Dance Project. I have studied both here and in Spain, and continue my studies (to keep current with the dance) at various workshops both here and abroad. I make it a point of really studying the different elements of the dance, especially el cante (singing) to teach my students the importance of the relationship between the dance and the singing. title: Spotlight Tour: Disavowed, with Julianne Wu ’28
description: On this tour, Julianne Wu ’28 will look at instances of disavowal in three works that illuminate, disturb, or challenge authority, including Bearded Man, Possibly Emperor Macrinus (Roman, early to mid-3rd century CE), Max Beckmann’s Self-Portrait in Tuxedo (1927), and High Street (1950) by Franz Kline. Spotlight Tours are designed and led by Harvard undergraduates from a range of academic disciplines. Each tour is focused on objects chosen by the student and provides visitors a unique, thematic view into the collections. Tours typically feature three works of art, embrace a conversational format, and last about 45 minutes. Open to the public, these tours start outside the museum shop on Saturdays and Sundays at 11am and 2pm. This program is supported by the Ho Family Student Guide Fund. The Ho Family Student Guide Program at the Harvard Art Museums prepares students to develop original, research-based tours. Through their training, Student Guides gain knowledge of the collections and develop skills in critical thinking, visual analysis, public speaking, and leadership. Find out what the Student Guides are up to anytime on Instagram @harvardarthappens.

description: This class is fun and challenging! We warm up, practice basic movements, and then assemble them into a sequence. N’golo from Angola, rhythms from Congo, and acrobatics from Guinea combined to form a martial art disguised as a dance and played like a game. All these elements plus a deliberate sense of fun result in a vigorous workout for the body and mind! I saw Capoeira played on the streets, and was curious to know more. I fell in love with the music, history, and movements of the style. I graduated as a Mestre in 1984 and moved to Boston in 1986. I was the first to teach Capoeira in New England. Mestre Joao Pequenho certified me as a teacher of Capoeira Angola in 1991. Contra Mestre Calango: I moved to Boston in 2000 to continue training with Mestre Deraldo. Since then, I traveled with him to universities and events around the world to assist in demonstrating and teaching of the beautiful art of Capoeira Angola. I graduated as a Contra Mestre in 2017. title: Man of Marble
description: Directed by Andrzej Wajda, 1977. The best and fiercest of Wajda’s ’70s political films, Man of Marble was stuck in development inferno for over a decade. Authorities greenlit the production in 1976, spurring Aleksander Ścibor-Rylski to update the script according to changed (which is to say liberalized) conditions of his present. Student director Agnieszka—Krystyna Janda in the first of four Wajda appearances—sets out to investigate the life of Mateusz Birkut, a Stakhanovite shock force worker in 1950s Nowa Huta who has since unceremoniously vanished. Newsreels, reenactment and absurdist fiction join forces in a bravado of critical cinema that obsessed masses at home and elsewhere. One fifth of Poland caught the 1977 theatrical release, while Jean-Luc Godard raved about Janda’s “critical eyes of freedom” in Cahiers du Cinéma . An inspired disassembly of myth, propaganda and media manipulation, the film was also instrumental in prefiguring (and fomenting) trade union movements that would roil the country only three years later. Part of the series Once There Was History . Andrzej Wajda at 100.

The brainchild of ace Boston guitarists Ryan Taylor and Johnny Trama, this collective, more than a mere homage, harness the Allman Brothers tradition as a vehicle to bring a unique and exciting experience every night. Matt Zeiner began his professional music career touring with Matt “Guitar” Murphy, who exposed him to a fusion of blues and jazz. His career took a significant turn in 2000 when Dickey Betts of the Allman Brothers Band recruited him as a keyboardist and vocalist, leading to a fruitful collaboration and tour. Zeiner’s own songwriting flourished during this time, contributing notably to the band’s repertoire. After four years touring, he returned home, focused on original material, and formed his own band. They achieved recognition with their 2007 release, “Live on a Summer Night,” and continued to evolve through collaborations with artists like Melvin Sparks and Jeff Pevar. Zeiner’s band has since been working on an ambitious new album, showcasing his ability to craft infectious melodies with tight, dynamic arrangements across a range of soul, R&B, and rock genres. Johnny Trama on guitar conjures up riffs and rhythms that speak volumes. His journey through the realms of rock, soul, and blues, playing with icons like Bettye LaVette and Jesse Dee, has armed him with a mystical musical prowess. Jesse Williams on bass has played with everyone from Duke Robillard, Louis Walker to North Mississippi Allstars. Tom Arey behind the drums has played with artists like Peter Wolf’s Midnight Travelers. Brendan Tommaney on percussion has played with groups like Pink Talking Fish, Tommaney and brings a jazz-infused sensibility that adds depth and dimension to the band’s sound.

description: Sh!t-Faced Shakespeare: Romeo & Juliet “Call me but love, and I’ll be new baptized.” There is no love lost between the Capulet and Montague families and everyone in Verona knows it. If any of this puts you off, maybe another show is more your speed. *Warning: But also, we do have sword fights, loud sounds, and flashing lights if those affect your person.* About Shit-faced Shakespeare®: An entirely serious Shakespeare play, with an entirely shit-faced cast member. The original, award winning, international smash-hit direct from London’s West End to an American theater near you! Founded in 2010 in the UK and first arriving on US shores back in 2015. Shit-faced Shakespeare® has delighted audiences all over the States with their highfalutin cocktail of traditional Elizabethan theater and balls-to-the-wall drunken shenanigans. Accept no poor relations, pale imitations or paltry recreations, see the authentic Shit-faced Shakespeare® show which started it all. Featuring a revolving cast of Boston’s finest actors, the choicest cuts of Shakespearian classics and more inebriated antics than you can violently shake a cod piece at. title: Bigfoot Research Organization
description: THE BIGFOOT RESEARCH ORGANIZATION Galadriel, in the Second Age of Middle Earth, sought to rid the realm of the Dark Lord Sauron with the power of her ring, Nenya, the Ring of Adamant. But Lo! The … …oh, sorry, wrong channel…we’re talking about Bigfoot… OK, let me just get this out of the way…y’all believe what you want…Bigfoot’s real, there’s plenty of evidence…we don’t need some freakin’ yahoo to go out there and blow one away just for the body…for years now, DNA samples, footprints, and mid-tarsal breaks and such have pushed the proverbial football of proof over the proverbial scrimmage line — way over, actually…if you’d just put aside your poo-poo-ing…all you have to do is spend some time watching the relevant “Monster Quest” episodes (specifically, S1E2, S1E5, S2E4, S2E20, S3E11, and S4E8) on YouTube… …hold on… …the point is: all that’s beside the point…we have serious crap to discuss about Tronald Dump and all his minions…and The Bigfoot Research Organization is ready — (somewhat) — to speak in a semi-informed manner about all the latest…uh…stuff…and to render into song what everyone hopes, time after time, will be a show-ending number… So, tell your extended family you have an errand to run and escape from the-side-show-that-is-your-Thanksgiving-hell-weekend and come spend Saturday evening with the-side-show-that-is-us-but-at-least-to-whom-you’re-not-related (praise god) — we are the chicken head stablization phenomenon (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HGqRrclxgIo) at the confluence of ever-shifting landscape of political discourse and social conscience and folk music worlds…the puzzling gaze that will not move, no matter how you contort the body… …and we’ve been practicing…a little. Don’t miss it. It’s like nothing you’ve never experienced before, plus some cool lighting and sound effects… AND…Passim now has a wine and beer license. You’re welcome, Rob, Lloyd, Dave (and Joel in absentia)

description: Club d'Elf returns to the Lizard Lounge with special guests Rob Compa and Vicente Lebron Nov 28th! Event is 21+ $30/$35 GA $80 reserved table Doors 6:30 Club d’Elf returns to the Lizard Lounge Nov 28th for two post Thanksgiving shows! The line up features Rob Compa (guitar), Mister Rourke (turntables), Paul Schultheis (keys) Mike Rivard (bass & sintir), Vicente Lebron (congas) and Dean Johnston (drums). The band played its first show at The Lizard in Feb 1998 and began a residency that ran until March 2020. The Lizard has always been home for d’Elf and the band loves to return whenever the opportunity arises. What begins as a groove in Club d’Elf’s world often becomes a doorway into someplace older, stranger and unshackled by time.The band has spent twenty seven years helping audiences lose track of time with its shape-shifting fusion of Moroccan trance, dub, electronica, jazz and improvised funk. Built around bassist and composer Mike Rivard, each performance features a rotating cast drawn from Boston, New York and beyond, creating a constantly shifting ecosystem where trance forms the central core of the band’s aesthetic. Under the tutelage of longtime member and Casablanca native Brahim Fribgane, the group absorbed Moroccan trance music deeply into its DNA. Fribgane passed away in early 2024, but his spirit remains embedded in the band’s sound, especially through Rivard’s commanding sintir work, learned under the guidance of Fribgane and Gnawa masters Hassan Hakmoun and Mahmoud Guinia. Their new album, Loon and Thrush (released 4/10/26), recorded entirely live in the studio with minimal overdubs, channels that lineage into a raw, improvisatory flight. While largely built on Rivard originals, the album continues the band’s tradition of honoring key influences, offering Moroccan-infused takes on Grateful Dead classics “Bird Song” and “New Speedway Boogie.” The overarching theme of the record is“flight” itself—the avian imagery of the title track, the Dead’s celesti

title: Spotlight Tour: Un/Settled, with Leandra Bautista ’28
description: On this tour, Leandra Bautista ’28 will look closely at three works of art that evoke home as a space of either comfort or discomfort. The stops on the tour are Woman on a Striped Sofa with a Dog (1876) by Mary Cassatt; a 12th-century Italian casket in the shape of a tower; and Robert Smullyan Sloan’s 1945 painting of a Black soldier. Spotlight Tours are designed and led by Harvard undergraduates from a range of academic disciplines. Each tour is focused on objects chosen by the student and provides visitors a unique, thematic view into the collections. Tours typically feature three works of art, embrace a conversational format, and last about 45 minutes. Open to the public, these tours start outside the museum shop on Saturdays and Sundays at 11am and 2pm. This program is supported by the Ho Family Student Guide Fund. The Ho Family Student Guide Program at the Harvard Art Museums prepares students to develop original, research-based tours. Through their training, Student Guides gain knowledge of the collections and develop skills in critical thinking, visual analysis, public speaking, and leadership. Find out what the Student Guides are up to anytime on Instagram @harvardarthappens.

description: Based on the true story of Katherine Ann Power and Clare Schroeder, this gripping new drama follows two women bound by a single, life-altering moment. It’s 1970. College student Power joins an activist group to protest the war. When their resistance turns deadly, Schroeder must grow up in the shadow of her father’s murder while Power disappears and spends decades on the FBI’s Most Wanted List. title: Spotlight Tour: Child’s Play, with Ricardo Fernandes Garcia ’27
description: Know Before You Go How to join: Check in at the Visitor Services desk; space is limited. Fee: This is a free event. Accessibility accommodations: If you would like to request accommodations for your visit, please contact Visitor Services at am_register@harvard.edu or 617-495-9400. For more details about accommodations at the museums, please see the Accessibility page.General info: The museum visit page has general guidelines for your visit. On this tour, Ricardo Fernandes Garcia ’27 will explore how representations of innocence have enabled artists to address conflict and war. The stops on the tour are Winslow Homer’s The Brush Harrow (1865), which depicts a scene from childhood; George Grosz’s Nutcracker(1931), which features a group of toys; and Joseph Cornell’s Midnight Carrousel (1954), which suggests the imagination at work. Spotlight Tours are designed and led by Harvard undergraduates from a range of academic disciplines. Each tour is focused on objects chosen by the student and provides visitors a unique, thematic view into the collections. Tours typically feature three works of art, embrace a conversational format, and last about 45 minutes. Open to the public, these tours start outside the museum shop on Saturdays and Sundays at 11am and 2pm. This program is supported by the Ho Family Student Guide Fund. The Ho Family Student Guide Program at the Harvard Art Museums prepares students to develop original, research-based tours. Through their training, Student Guides gain knowledge of the collections and develop skills in critical thinking, visual analysis, public speaking, and leadership. Find out what the Student Guides are up to anytime on Instagram @harvardarthappens.

title: Wałęsa: Man of Hope
description: Directed by Andrzej Wajda, 2013. “This film is going to be the hardest of my career,” intimated Andrzej Wajda during preproduction on Wałęsa: Man of Hope . “I don’t want to, but I have to [make it],” the director quipped, using Lech Wałęsa’s own words about running for president in 1990. Almost two decades Wałęsa’s senior, Wajda was eighty-seven at the film’s premiere; he would go on to finish one last feature, the extraordinary Afterimage in 2016. A late addition to what the filmmaker called his Solidarity “triptych,” Wałęsa is an uncommonly propulsive biopic of the union leader, Nobel laureate and democratic statesman, who reportedly approved of Wajda’s portrayal. As in Man of Marble and Man of Iron , documentary and reportage are interlaced with fictional scenarios of Wałęsa (mostly) excelling in the public and private sphere. Robert Więckiewicz shines as the titular rebel, showing late Wajda in good control of cast, crew and national legend. Part of the series Once There Was History . Andrzej Wajda at 100.

title: Harvard Square French Fry & Pairings Food Tour
description: Harvard Square is famous for so much — Harvard University, eclectic bookshops, buskers, and a food scene that punches well above its weight. But here’s what most visitors don’t know: it’s also home to some of the best french fries in all of Massachusetts . Together with our guide Larom, a Harvard alum, we built an entire tour around that fact, and it’s become one of the most unique food experiences in Cambridge. On this 90-minute walking adventure, you’ll sample distinctly different styles of fries at three beloved Harvard Square spots — from classic hand-cut wedges to smoky BBQ fries to legendary sweet potato fries — each paired with a drink chosen specifically to bring out the flavors. We’ll try the original raspberry lime rickey , a refreshing peach lemonade , and a crazy ice cream frappe that has to be seen to be believed. All pairings are non-alcoholic, making this tour genuinely fun for the whole family. Along the way, your guide will walk you through the beloved cobblestone streets past Harvard Yard , the Widener Library , the quirky Harvard Lampoon building , and the storied Harvard Faculty Club — sharing the funny, fresh, and occasionally absurd stories that make this neighborhood unlike anywhere else in Boston. You’ll also hear the full saga of the French Fry Wars of the late 20th Century , a deliciously bizarre chapter of local food history that explains why Harvard Square’s fry scene is what it is today. This food tour is ideal for: Visitors to Boston looking for a memorable, off-the-beaten-path Cambridge experience Families with kids and teens who want something interactive and delicious Date nights — quirky, fun, and plenty of good food Birthday celebrations and small group outings Local students, grad students, alums, and neighbors who want to see a new side of Harvard!

title: Public Research Talk: Plato, the American Genius: The Life of Emerson's Orient
description: Registration is required. Please register to attend in person . Please register to attend on Zoom . For nearly a century, scholars have traced the influence of Asian thought on American Transcendentalism. Building on this scholarship, this talk examines Emerson’s construction of the Orient and the role it played in the larger metaphysical geography of his thought. Emerson’s encounter with Asian traditions was mediated by a Platonic understanding of East and West, a dialectic he believed was approaching a new historical threshold in America. Plato furnished the philosophical framework through which Emerson brought Confucius, Hindu scripture, Persian poetry, and European mysticism into a shared intellectual horizon. Within this framework, Emerson imagined the emergence of a distinctly American genius, liberated from the inherited geographical and philosophical divisions of Eurasia. Finally, the talk follows Emerson’s reception in China, where his philosophy of individuality enters into contemporary debates over Confucian tradition, personal freedom, and political authority. Here, nearly two centuries after his emergence in Concord, Emerson remains a dangerous thinker. Simon Cox received his PhD in the Study of Religion from Rice University in 2019 and is the author of The Subtle Body: A Genealogy (Oxford University Press, 2022). He is a Research Fellow at the Esalen Center for Theory and Research and a Visiting Scholar at the Center for the Study of World Religions at Harvard Divinity School. His research focuses on the intellectual history of subtle body traditions, with particular attention to the parallel genealogies of the Western concept of energy and the Chinese concept of qi . Bringing together the history of religions, philosophy, and intellectual history, his work explores how these traditions have shaped changing conceptions of the body, consciousness, and cosmology across Eurasia. His research project at the CSWR develops a dual genealogy of energy and qi ,

title: Man of Iron
description: Directed by Andrzej Wajda, 1981. “Why don’t you make a film about us? Call it: Man of Iron .” Wajda’s incendiary sequel to Man of Marble emerged after the director’s encounter with shipyard workers in Gdańsk, where a 1980 strike led to the establishment of Solidarity—Poland’s first independent trade union. Real-life organizers Lech Wałęsa and Anna Walentynowicz appear as themselves in a rough-and-ready cine-pamphlet shot in the immediate aftermath of (what seemed to be) a victorious direct action. The son of original protagonist Birkut takes center stage in a time-hopping narrative which, like its predecessor, blends fiction and documentary into a potion wholly its own. That the experiment was successful is testified by anecdotes of electrified viewers singing the national anthem after screenings. As a result, Wajda was pleased: “Was the film good or bad? What does it matter? There was no film like it.” Feeling (rightly) endangered, the government quickly ensured no other such work could emerge by imposing harsh martial law for the next two years. Part of the series Once There Was History . Andrzej Wajda at 100. Screening on film.

description: ” Doing something different with a pop song, breaking the convention of verses and choruses– it’s something we always keep in mind when we’re recording,” says bassist Tom Warmsley, who founded Temples with singer/guitarist James Bagshaw in the summer of 2012. Looking like a West Coast psych band, Temples bear all the hallmarks of cosmic travellers. There’s the band name, for starters, there are track titles that sound like JG Ballard novels (Prisms, The Golden Throne, Sun Structures) and there’s the fact that they take incense sticks on the road with them. The Kettering four-piece’s music is a mix of scuzzy glam stomp, dreamy, 12-string-drenched folk-rock, droning psych and more – all given a 2013 spin. Retro is a dirty word.

He started on clarinet when he was eight, switching to alto at 12, and finally to tenor two years later. Bergonzi was inspired early on by Sonny Rollins, Coltrane, and Hank Mobley. He attended Lowell University and then after graduation played electric bass in local bands behind singers and strippers, saving up enough money to move to New York in 1972. After struggling in the Big Apple for seven years and gaining some recognition as a member of Two Generations of Brubeck and of the Dave Brubeck Quartet (with whom he appeared on several Concord albums during 1979-1981), Bergonzi moved back to Boston in 1981, where he developed a strong career both as a tenorman and as an educator. Majestic Healing Pathways™ is the foundational care model that guides all of Majestic Community Wellness’s programs. title: Online Seminar On Undergraduate Mathematics Education
description: Speaker: Nathan Alexander (Howard University) Title: critstats: Reimagining introductory statistics using a critical quantitative approach Abstract: I describe a modern approach to teaching introductory statistics that leverages logic, theory, and computational methods to engage students in critical quantitative analysis. I explore how integrating open-source software tools into this curriculum enables learners to participate in an interdisciplinary process of knowledge construction: defining terms and propositions and applying statistical concepts to social issues.
